pinneapple_design.aero.aircraft
children.doc:
From a section polar to aircraft numbers: top speed, CO2 per 100 km, stall speed, and the design constraints.

A light single-engine propeller aircraft (defaults: Cessna 172 class). The wing uses the section polar with an
elliptic-loading induced drag CL^2/(pi e AR); the rest of the airplane is a fixed CD0. Piston power lapses with
altitude (Gagg-Ferrar), fuel from the brake-specific fuel consumption, CO2 from the fuel burnt.

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.aircraft3d
children.doc:
The whole aircraft in 3D: vortex lattice (wing + tail, trimmed), section drag strip by strip from the CFD
surrogate, fuselage and tail drag by component build-up (Raymer), wing and tail weights (Raymer, general aviation),
centre of gravity, neutral point with the fuselage's destabilising moment, stall by the critical-section method.

Requirements a design must meet: stall speed, stall starting inboard (not at the tips), static margin, trim with the
tail, spar depth, span. Objectives: top speed, CO2 per 100 km, stall speed.

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.aircraft_surrogate
children.doc:
A surrogate of the aerodynamics of a whole 3-D aircraft, trained, used and graded in one call.

    from pinneapple_design.aero.aircraft_surrogate import aircraft_surrogate_study
    r = aircraft_surrogate_study("out/")     # out/aircraft_surrogate.mp4, out/aircraft_field.glb + .json, figures

What happens inside, every number measured in the call:

1. **Data from the solver.** Designs of the library's light aircraft (wing area, aspect ratio, taper, leading-edge
   sweep, tip twist) are drawn by a Latin hypercube; each one is solved once by the vortex lattice of wing +
   horizontal tail (:func:`~pinneapple_design.aero.vlm.solve`), and the solution, linear in the angle of attack,
   gives the pressure jump ``dCp`` on every one of its 200 panels at several angles. Some designs train the model,
   the others are held out and never seen in training.
2. **The surrogate.** A bagged ensemble of networks maps the five design parameters and the angle of attack to the
   whole ``dCp`` field; the spread of the ensemble is its uncertainty. The panel layout is the same for every
   design, so the field is a fixed-size vector.
3. **Physics-consistent coefficients.** CL and Cm (Kutta-Joukowski on the bound vortices) and CDi (Trefftz plane)
   are computed from the *predicted* field with the solver's own post-processing
   (:func:`~pinneapple_design.aero.vlm.loads_from_circulation`), so the coefficients and the field never disagree.
4. **Inference against the data.** On the held-out designs, the prediction is compared with the solver and with
   the nearest training design (a lookup baseline), and one design outside the trained ranges is checked for an
   out-of-distribution flag.
5. **VeriPhysics grade.** The checks below decide APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT with the library's grading policy
   (:func:`pinneapple_veriphysics.policy.decide`): ``grade.reference`` (field error on held-out designs),
   ``grade.applicability`` (in-range designs accepted, the out-of-range one flagged), ``grade.robustness``
   (smooth response to small input changes), and the aerodynamic checks ``aero.lift_from_field``,
   ``aero.linearity_alpha`` (the lattice is linear in the angle of attack), ``aero.symmetry`` (left and right
   wing carry the same load) and ``aero.munk_bound`` (span efficiency at most 1).

The vortex lattice is inviscid, small-angle and has no fuselage: the surrogate learns that model, not a viscous
flow. Needs torch and matplotlib; the MP4 needs ffmpeg (on the PATH, or through ``imageio-ffmpeg``).

functions.name: aircraft_surrogate_study
functions.sig: (out_dir: str = 'aircraft_surrogate', n_train: int = 48, n_test: int = 12, n_alpha: int = 6, epochs: int = 1500, frames: int = 80, fps: int = 10, width_px: int = 1280, seed: int = 0, bounds: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None, target: dict[str, float] | None = None, probe: dict[str, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Train a surrogate of the 3-D aircraft's aerodynamics on vortex-lattice data, compare its inferences with the
solver and the training data, and grade it with VeriPhysics.

Parameters
----------
out_dir : str
    Folder for the video, the 3-D field view and the figures (a job runner passes its own output folder).
n_train : int
    Aircraft geometries in the training set (each solved once, sampled at ``n_alpha`` angles).
n_test : int
    Held-out geometries, never seen in training.
n_alpha : int
    Angles of attack per geometry, stratified over -2..8 deg.
epochs : int
    Training epochs of the ensemble (full batch).
frames : int
    Frames of the training video (snapshots spaced geometrically over the epochs).
fps : int [1/s]
    Frames per second of the video.
width_px : int [px]
    Width of the video and figures.
seed : int
    Seed of the designs, the split and the networks.
bounds : dict, optional
    The design space (default :data:`BOUNDS`): the box the designs are drawn from, the model's declared validity.
target : dict, optional
    The user's design (the five geometry parameters and ``alpha``), shown in the video and the 3-D view; by
    default the first held-out design at 6 deg.
probe : dict, optional
    A request checked for applicability (default :data:`PROBE`, outside the default design space).

Returns
-------
dict
    ``outputs`` (the measured numbers), ``checks`` (code, status, detail, value), ``decision`` (VeriPhysics
    verdict and reasons), ``files`` (names written in ``out_dir``).

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.aircraft_surrogate_demo
children.doc:
From a sentence to a verified 3-D aircraft aerodynamics surrogate, shown where VeriPhysics rejects it and where it
accepts it (#1438).

The demo starts from a plain-text request: no geometry, no data. :func:`parse_request` reads the planform and the
angle of attack from the text (Portuguese or English) and says which values it did not find. The same request then
goes through three rounds of :func:`pinneapple_design.aero.aircraft_surrogate.aircraft_surrogate_study`:

1. a quick model, few designs and a short training: VeriPhysics grades it and rejects it;
2. the full dataset over the library's design space: the model is approved, but the requested design is outside the
   space it was trained and validated on, so the request is rejected by the applicability gate;
3. the design space extended to cover the request, with new solver data: the model is approved and the request is
   accepted; its error is then measured against the solver.

An acceptance map (aspect ratio x sweep) shows, cell by cell, where each model accepts or rejects a request, with the
solver's error for every cell. When Blender's Python module (``bpy``) is installed, Cycles renders the aircraft with
the pressure jump on its lifting surfaces and the vortex-lattice streamlines, tip vortices included; the
streamlines of a surrogate's render come from the circulation that surrogate predicts. Everything is put together in
one MP4 with ffmpeg.

functions.name: parse_request
functions.sig: (text: str) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Read the design from a plain-text request.

Each design value is the first number after one of its names (PT or EN: "alongamento 12", "aspect ratio of 12",
"enflechamento de 15°", "ângulo de ataque 4 graus"); a decimal comma is read as a point. A value the text does not
give is taken from :data:`DEFAULT_REQUEST` and listed in ``defaulted``; a value outside what the lattice and the
airframe model can take (:data:`PHYSICAL`) is clipped and listed in ``clipped``. "Washout of 3°" is a tip twist
of -3°.

Returns
-------
dict
    ``design`` (the six values), ``found`` / ``defaulted`` / ``clipped`` (names), ``lang`` ("pt" or "en").

functions.name: extend_bounds
functions.sig: (bounds: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], design: dict[str, float], margin: float = 0.15) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]
functions.doc:
The design space grown to contain ``design``: each value outside its range moves that end past the value by
``margin`` of the range's original width (clipped to :data:`PHYSICAL`).

functions.name: request_verdict
functions.sig: (model_verdict: str, flagged: bool) -> str
functions.doc:
A request is answered only by an approved model, and only inside the space that model was validated on:
REJECT when the model is rejected or the request is flagged outside its domain, else the model's verdict.

functions.name: acceptance_map
functions.sig: (models: dict[str, Any], design: dict[str, float], n: int = 8, ar: tuple[float, float] | None = None, sweep: tuple[float, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
For an ``n`` x ``n`` grid of aspect ratio x sweep (the other values from ``design``), each model's
applicability flag and its field error against the solver.

Returns
-------
dict
    ``ar``, ``sweep`` (grid axes), ``error`` and ``accepted`` per model name (n x n arrays, [sweep, ar]),
    ``solver_seconds``.

functions.name: cinematic_available
functions.sig: () -> bool
functions.doc:
Whether Blender's Python module is installed. Found, not imported: Blender is only ever imported in the child
process that renders (:func:`_in_child`); importing it in the caller, often a worker thread, can crash it.

functions.name: aircraft_surrogate_demo
functions.sig: (request: str = '', out_dir: str = 'aircraft_surrogate_demo', rounds: int = 3, n_train: tuple[int, int, int] = (8, 48, 64), epochs: tuple[int, int, int] = (150, 1500, 1500), n_test: int = 12, n_alpha: int = 6, frames: int = 50, fps: int = 10, width_px: int = 1280, map_n: int = 8, cinematic: str = 'auto', orbit_frames: int = 28, render_scale: float = 1.0, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
From a plain-text request to a 3-D aircraft aerodynamics surrogate graded by VeriPhysics, shown where the
grade rejects it and where it accepts it.

Parameters
----------
request : str
    The problem in words (Portuguese or English), e.g. "a light aircraft with a slender wing: aspect ratio 12,
    sweep 15°, at 4° angle of attack". No geometry: the airframe is the library's light aircraft with the
    planform the text gives (:func:`parse_request`).
out_dir : str
    Folder for the video, the renders, the figures and the 3-D field view.
rounds : int
    1 to 3: the quick model, the full model on the library's design space, the design space extended to cover
    the request.
n_train : tuple of int
    Training geometries of each round.
epochs : tuple of int
    Training epochs of each round.
n_test : int
    Held-out geometries of each round, never seen in training.
n_alpha : int
    Angles of attack per geometry.
frames : int
    Snapshots in each round's training video.
fps : int [1/s]
    Frame rate of the training videos.
width_px : int [px]
    Width of the videos and figures.
map_n : int
    Cells per side of the acceptance map (each solved by the lattice).
cinematic : str
    "auto" (Cycles renders when ``bpy`` is installed), "on", "fast" or "off". "fast" is the same renders at a
    lower cost (:data:`FAST_RENDER`: at most 0.6 of the resolution, fewer samples, at most 12 orbit frames), for a
    run that has to fit a short job limit.
orbit_frames : int
    Frames of the Cycles camera move.
render_scale : float
    Scale of the Cycles resolution (1 is 1280 x 720 for the stills, 960 x 540 for the camera move).
seed : int
    Seed of every round's designs and networks.

Returns
-------
dict
    ``request`` (the parsed design), ``rounds`` (each round's verdicts, checks and numbers), ``map`` (acceptance
    per model), ``checks`` (the demo's own, measured), ``outputs``, ``files`` (in ``out_dir``).

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.airliner3d
children.doc:
Airliner physics (A320 class): cruise at transonic Mach and the low-speed end, for the whole aircraft.

Cruise: vortex lattice with the Prandtl-Glauert stretch (x / beta) for compressibility, trimmed with the tail; section
drag strip by strip = friction at the real Reynolds number + the form-drag increment from the CFD section surrogate
(its drag above flat-plate friction at the training Reynolds number); wave drag per strip from the Korn equation with
Lock's rule (simple-sweep theory); fuselage, nacelles, fin by component build-up (Raymer). Mission: Breguet range with
a turbofan's specific fuel consumption, MTOW iterated with the wing weight (Raymer, transport). Low speed: wing CLmax
from the section cl max (critical section, vortex lattice) plus high-lift devices, approach speed Vref = 1.23 Vs.

Requirements: span (ICAO code C gate, 36 m), approach speed, 1.3 g buffet margin, fuel volume in the wing box, static
margin, stall starting inboard, trim, thickness. Objectives: CO2 per passenger-km, cruise Mach, approach speed.

OpenFOAM case for one airfoil at one angle of attack: simpleFoam, k-omega SST resolved to the wall (y+ < 1).

Non-dimensional: chord 1, |U| = 1, nu = 1/Re. Far field with freestream conditions, forces with forceCoeffs about the

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.optimize
children.doc:
Design search: NSGA-II over airfoil shape + wing area on the surrogate, with feasibility and trust per design.

Three objectives: top speed (up), CO2 per 100 km (down) and stall speed (down: shorter runways, gentler landings).
Speed and CO2 both come from low drag; what they fight is the low-speed side, so the front is speed vs stall speed.

Each candidate gets a section polar from the MLP ensemble (fast, with a spread), aircraft performance from it, the
requirement checks, and a trust level. The graph network adds the flow field and a second, independent set of
coefficients for the designs you look at; OpenFOAM is the last word (see :mod:`.verify`).

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.panel
children.doc:
Hess-Smith panel method: incompressible, inviscid (potential) flow around an airfoil.

Constant-strength source panels plus one vortex strength shared by every panel; the flow-tangency condition at each
panel's midpoint and the Kutta condition (equal and opposite tangential velocities on the two trailing-edge panels)
give N + 1 equations for the N source strengths and the vortex strength. Written from the textbook formulation
(Hess & Smith 1967; Moran, "An Introduction to Theoretical and Computational Aerodynamics", 1984, ch. 4).

It is the inviscid reference for the airfoil benchmark: what any potential-flow model, a PINN included, can at best
reach (Cl without viscous decambering, zero drag by d'Alembert's paradox), and a check that such a model has solved
its own equations. Units: chord 1, free stream 1.

classes.name: PanelResult
classes.doc:
The panel solution (chord 1, free stream 1).

Attributes
----------
alpha_deg : float [deg]
    Angle of attack.
cp : np.ndarray [-]
    Pressure coefficient at the panel mid-points.
cl_kutta_joukowski : float [-]
    Lift coefficient from the circulation.
cl_pressure : float [-]
    Lift coefficient from the pressure.
cd_pressure : float [-]
    Pressure drag coefficient (zero in exact potential flow).
cm_quarter : float [-]
    Pitching moment about the quarter chord.

methods.name: velocity
methods.doc: Velocity (u, v) at arbitrary points outside the airfoil.

functions.name: airfoil_nodes
functions.sig: (shape: np.ndarray, n_per_side: int = 100, close_te: bool = False) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Clockwise panel nodes: lower surface trailing edge -> leading edge, then upper leading edge -> trailing edge,
cosine-clustered at both ends. The blunt trailing edge of the CST shapes stays open (a gap of 0.25 % chord)
unless ``close_te``: then both end nodes move to the mid-point of the gap. With the gap open the Kutta condition
acts on panels that shrink below the gap as the panels are refined and Cl drifts down by about 0.8 % per
doubling (NACA 2412, 4 deg: 0.728, 0.723, 0.717, 0.712, 0.706 for 50-800 panels per side); closed, it converges
(0.745, 0.734, 0.731, 0.7296, 0.7292).

Solve the potential flow around an airfoil given by CST ``shape`` (or by clockwise ``nodes``);
``close_te``: close the blunt CST trailing edge (see :func:`airfoil_nodes`), needed for a grid-converged Cl.

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.surrogate
children.doc:
Surrogates for the airfoil flow: a MeshGraphNet on the CFD grid (fields + Cl, Cd, Cm) and an MLP ensemble.

The graph is a subset of the O-grid cells near the airfoil (every 2nd cell around, ~24 levels from the wall out to
~5 chords), so every design has the same nodes and edges and only the coordinates change. Edges join neighbours on
that lattice plus longer jumps (multi-scale), so a few message-passing rounds reach across the near field.

Node inputs: position, log wall distance, level, wall flag, free-stream direction, and the shape weights.
Node outputs: p, Ux, Uy, log(1 + nut/nu). A pooled readout over the wall nodes gives Cl, Cd, Cm.

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.train
children.doc:
Train the airfoil surrogates on OpenFOAM runs and measure them on shapes they never saw.

Two models from :mod:`.surrogate`: the :class:`~.surrogate.MLPEnsemble` on (shape, alpha) -> (Cl, log Cd, Cm),
bootstrapped so its spread is an uncertainty, and the :class:`~.surrogate.AeroGNN` (MeshGraphNet; Pfaff et al.,
"Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks", ICLR 2021) on the near-wall O-grid cells, which predicts the
fields p, Ux, Uy, log(1 + nut/nu) and the coefficients.

The split is by shape, not by run (:func:`split`): a held-out shape is unseen at every angle, so the test error is the
error on a new design. The NACA reference polars are a second, independent test.

    recs = load_runs(["runs/"])                       # run records of pinneapple_design.aero.dataset
    bundle, metrics = train_surrogates(recs, gnn_minutes=60)
    torch.save(bundle, "surrogate.pt")                # what pinneapple_design.aero.optimize.Engine.load reads

The CLI is ``apps/aero_optimizer/tools/train_surrogate.py``.

functions.sig: (tr: Sequence[dict[str, Any]], te: Sequence[dict[str, Any]], minutes: float | None = 60.0, seed: int = 0, batch: int = 4, log: Callable[[str], Any] = print, *, epochs: int | None = None, hidden: int = 48, mp: int = 8, layout: Layout | None = None, checkpoint_dir: str | None = None, checkpoint_every: int = 5)
functions.doc:
Train the graph network on ``tr`` for a wall-clock budget of ``minutes`` and/or a number of ``epochs``.

The learning rate follows a cosine from 1e-3 to 3e-5 over the budget (the larger of the elapsed time and epoch
fractions). Every 5 epochs and at the end the Cd error on ``te`` is logged. Returns
``(model, norm, history, layout)``.

With ``checkpoint_dir``, the full training state (weights, optimiser, epoch, elapsed time, history, shuffling RNG)
is written to ``checkpoint_dir/gnn_last.pt`` every ``checkpoint_every`` epochs, and a later call with the same
settings resumes from it: an interrupted run continues to the same weights as an uninterrupted one. A
checkpoint written with other settings is refused.

Split, train both surrogates and measure them. Returns ``(bundle, metrics)``.

``bundle`` is the dict :meth:`.optimize.Engine.load` reads (``torch.save`` it); ``metrics`` holds the counts,
:func:`metrics` per model on the held-out shapes (``*_test``) and the NACA references (``*_reference``), the
per-run points and the graph network's training history. ``gnn_from`` reuses the graph network (and its
metrics, from the ``.metrics.json`` next to it) of an earlier bundle; ``gnn_minutes = 0`` (and no
``gnn_epochs``) skips it.

The aircraft numbers of a design (top speed, CO2 per 100 km, stall speed, cruise L/D) are recomputed from the

surrogate error. The runs use the training-set record format (set "verify", :mod:`.dataset`), so they can be added
to the next training (active learning). The CLI is ``apps/aero_optimizer/tools/verify.py``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.vlm
children.doc:
Vortex lattice method for the wing + horizontal tail of an Airframe.

Horseshoe vortices (bound leg on the panel quarter chord, trailing legs to downstream infinity along x), control points
at the panel three-quarter chord with the camber-line slope, twist and dihedral in the normals. The solution is linear
in the angle of attack and the tail incidence, so three solves give everything: lift, moment and the spanwise loading
as linear functions, induced drag (Trefftz plane) as a quadratic one. Trim, neutral point, stall station and drag at
any flight condition are then cheap.

Axes as the airframe: x aft, y right, z up. Free stream at angle alpha: V = (cos a, 0, sin a) * (-1) relative to the
aircraft moving forward, i.e. the air comes from -x... we use the usual aero convention with the air flowing towards
+x: V_inf = (cos a, 0, sin a).

methods.name: trim
methods.doc: (alpha, i_t) in radians giving this CL with zero pitching moment.

methods.name: neutral_point
methods.doc: x of the neutral point (aircraft, fixed tail incidence).

functions.name: build_lattice
functions.sig: (af, nc: int = 5, ns_wing: int = 14, ns_tail: int = 6, tail: bool = True) -> Lattice

functions.name: horseshoe_induced
functions.sig: (P, L: Lattice, legs = True)

functions.name: solve
functions.sig: (af, x_ref: float, nc: int = 5, ns_wing: int = 14, ns_tail: int = 6, tail: bool = True) -> VLMSolution

functions.name: trefftz
functions.sig: (L: Lattice) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Trefftz-plane normal wash per unit strip circulation ``Wn`` (ns, ns) and strip edge lengths ``ln`` (ns,).

Geometry only: the induced drag of any strip circulation ``g`` (per unit free-stream speed) is
``CDi = sum_ij g_i (-Wn_ij) g_j ln_i / S``. :func:`solve` and :func:`loads_from_circulation` use it.

functions.name: loads_from_circulation
functions.sig: (L: Lattice, gamma: np.ndarray, s_ref: float, c_ref: float, x_ref: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
CL, Cm (about ``x_ref``) and CDi of one panel circulation ``gamma`` (N,), per unit free-stream speed.

The same post-processing as :func:`solve`: Kutta-Joukowski on the bound legs with the free stream for lift and
moment, the Trefftz plane for induced drag. ``solve(...).coefficients(a, i_t)`` equals this function applied
to ``G.T @ [1, a, i_t]``.

functions.name: streamlines
functions.sig: (sol: VLMSolution, alpha: float, it: float, seeds: np.ndarray, steps: int = 220, h: float = 0.08, core: float = 0.08) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Potential-flow streamlines (free stream + horseshoe vortices, desingularised with a core radius).
The wake is the flat horseshoe sheet: it shows the downwash and the swirl around the tips, not the roll-up.
Returns (n_seeds, steps+1, 3).

children.name: pinneapple_design.aero.wing_design
children.doc:
Closed-loop wing design: the vortex lattice and a friction drag build-up, a learned model only when it pays off,
optimisation of the planform, and the design re-verified (#1181).

Design variables: aspect ratio, taper ratio and tip twist (washout) at a fixed wing area. For each design:

* **Vortex lattice** (:mod:`.vlm`, wing alone): the lift is linear in the angle of attack, so one solve gives the
  cruise and the landing condition: angle for the required lift coefficient, induced drag in the Trefftz plane, span
  efficiency ``e = CL^2 / (pi AR CDi)`` and the spanwise loading.
* **Profile drag**: turbulent flat-plate friction ``Cf = 0.455 / (log10 Re)^2.58 / (1 + 0.144 M^2)^0.65`` on the mean
  chord, the form factor ``FF = (1 + 0.6/(x/c)_m t/c + 100 (t/c)^4) (1.34 M^0.18 cos^0.28 sweep)`` and the wetted area
  ``S (1.977 + 0.52 t/c)`` (Raymer, *Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach*, 6th ed., eqs. 12.27, 12.30, 7.9).
* **Root bending moment** of the half wing from the lattice's loading, ``M = q sum cl c y dy`` over the strips at the
  angle that pulls ``n_load`` g at cruise speed (a manoeuvre: the loading shape follows the angle), the structural
  limit.
* **Stall margin**: the largest local ``cl`` at the landing lift coefficient against the section's ``cl_max`` (a
  measured value of the section, given by the caller): the station that stalls first, and whether it is the tip.

The objective is the cruise drag ``q S (CD0 + CDi)``; the limits are the root bending moment, the stall margin and
the span. The design is re-verified with a finer lattice (convergence), against Munk's bound ``e <= 1`` and against
Prandtl's lifting line on the same planform. An OpenFOAM polar of the section is the next fidelity
(:mod:`.verify`); without the solver in the environment it is reported as not run.

lattice solve (about 30 ms).

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks
pinneapple_design.bricks.assembly
children.doc:
Grid assemblies of interlocking bricks: placement, stud-tube connectivity and validity rules.

Coordinates: ``x``, ``y`` in stud pitches (8 mm), ``z`` in plate heights (3.2 mm), z up, the ground at ``z = 0``.
A brick at ``(x, y, z)`` with footprint ``sx`` x ``sy`` covers the cells ``[x, x + sx) x [y, y + sy)`` and the
plate layers ``[z, z + h)``; ``rot = 1`` turns it a quarter turn about z (``sx, sy = ny, nx``).

Two bricks are connected where the top of the lower one (``z_a + h_a = z_b``) overlaps the footprint of the upper
one: every overlapping cell is one stud-tube contact. A brick on ``z = 0`` rests on the ground, which is either
a table (smooth, friction only) or a baseplate (studs everywhere), optionally limited to some rectangles (a table
edge, the two banks of a gap).

methods.name: box_mm
methods.doc: Lower and upper corners of the body in millimetres (cell bounds, without the 0.1 mm clearance).

classes.name: Ground
classes.doc:
``kind``: ``"table"`` (smooth, friction ``mu``) or ``"baseplate"`` (studs). ``regions``: rectangles in stud
units where the ground exists (``None`` = everywhere).

classes.name: Connection
classes.doc:
Contact between ``lower`` (brick index, ``-1`` = ground) and ``upper`` at plate height ``z``.

``rect``: overlap of the two footprints [stud units]; ``studs``: the cells (stud centres at ``i + 0.5``) where a
stud of the lower part enters the upper one (empty for a smooth contact).

classes.name: Assembly
classes.sig: (bricks: Sequence[Brick] | None = None, ground: Ground | None = None, name: str = '')
classes.doc:
A list of bricks on a stud grid plus the ground they stand on.

>>> a = Assembly()
>>> a.add("brick_2x4", 0, 0, 0)
0
>>> a.add("brick_2x2", 1, 0, 3, colour="blue")
1
>>> [(c.lower, c.upper, len(c.studs)) for c in a.connections()]
[(-1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 4)]

methods.doc: Pairs of bricks that share a cell (an impossible build).

methods.name: connections
methods.doc: Ground contacts and brick-on-brick contacts, with the stud cells of each.

methods.name: graph
methods.doc: Adjacency of the contact graph (node ``-1`` is the ground).

methods.doc: Bricks with a contact path to the ground.

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.closed_form
children.doc:
Closed-form references for brick statics (used to validate :mod:`.statics`, :mod:`.dynamics` and :mod:`.fea`).

* Tipping: a rigid body on a smooth support stands while its centre of mass is over the support polygon.
* Harmonic stacking of n identical unconnected blocks of length L: the block k-th from the top overhangs the one
  below it by L / (2 k), so the top block overhangs the table edge by (L / 2) H_n (H_n the n-th harmonic number).
  Johnson, "Leaning Tower of Lire", Am. J. Phys. 23, 240 (1955); Paterson and Zwick, "Overhang", Am. Math.
  Monthly 116(1), 19-44 (2009). This is the optimum for one block per level.
* Stud cantilever: a part hanging off the edge of a fixed one, held by a row of studs at x_s inside the contact
  patch [x0, x1], pivots about the outer edge x1. With weight W at x = d > x1 the most favourable distribution
  loads every stud equally: t = W (d - x1) / sum_s (x1 - x_s).
* Simply supported beam of span L, self-weight w per length and a central load P: reactions P / 2 + w L / 2,
  bending moment M(x) = (P / 2 + w L / 2) x - w x^2 / 2 for x <= L / 2, and Euler-Bernoulli mid-span deflection
  P L^3 / (48 E I) + 5 w L^4 / (384 E I), I = second moment of area.

functions.name: harmonic
functions.sig: (n: int) -> float

functions.name: harmonic_overhang
functions.sig: (n: int, length: float) -> float
functions.doc: Maximum overhang of ``n`` unconnected identical blocks, one per level: (L / 2) H_n.

functions.name: harmonic_stack
functions.sig: (n: int, length: float, edge: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Left-edge x positions of the blocks (bottom first) of the harmonic stack on a table ending at ``edge``.

functions.name: tip_over_offset
functions.sig: (length: float) -> float
functions.doc: Largest overhang of a single uniform block on a table edge: half its length.

functions.name: stud_cantilever_tension
functions.sig: (weight: float, d: float, studs_x: Sequence[float], x1: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Equal tension per stud [N] that holds a part of weight ``weight`` [N] with its centre of mass at ``d``,
pivoting about the patch edge ``x1`` (0 if the centre of mass is inside the patch).

functions.name: beam_reactions
functions.sig: (span: float, w: float, P: float) -> float
functions.doc: Each support reaction of a symmetric simply supported beam [N].

functions.name: beam_moment
functions.sig: (x: float, span: float, w: float, P: float) -> float
functions.doc: Bending moment at ``x`` (from a support) of the simply supported beam with a central load [N mm].

functions.name: beam_midspan_deflection
functions.sig: (span: float, E: float, inertia: float, P: float = 0.0, w: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc: Euler-Bernoulli mid-span deflection of a simply supported beam (consistent units).

functions.name: tower_tip_force
functions.sig: (weight: float, half_base: float, height: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Horizontal force at ``height`` that tips a rigid block of weight ``weight`` about the base edge at
``half_base`` from its centre of mass line: F = W b / h.

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.dynamics
children.doc:
Rigid-body replay of a brick build with NVIDIA Newton (:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics`).

Every cluster of parts held together by intact stud joints is one rigid body made of the parts' boxes (welded to the
world when a baseplate holds it); released joints become ordinary box-box contacts with friction.
The ground is Newton's plane, or static table boxes for ground regions (then the plane is a floor below them, so
parts that leave the table fall onto it). Newton handles box-box contacts with Coulomb friction (XPBD by default).

The static analysis (:mod:`.statics`) decides which joints fail; this module shows what happens next. Newton has
no breakable joints, so a joint either holds for the whole replay or is released from the start.

functions.name: table_boxes
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, margin_mm: float = 80.0) -> list[tuple[float, float, float, float]]
functions.doc: The ground regions clipped to the build's neighbourhood, (x0, x1, y0, y1) in millimetres.

functions.name: clusters
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, broken: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = ()) -> tuple[list[list[int]], set[int]]
functions.doc: Groups of bricks held together by intact stud joints, and the groups welded to a baseplate.

functions.name: rigid_scene
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, broken: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = (), joint: JointModel | None = None, dead_loads: Sequence = ())
functions.doc:
Newton :class:`RigidScene` of the build (metres): one rigid body per cluster of bricks held by intact stud
joints (a compound of their boxes), welded to the world when it is held by a baseplate. ``dead_loads``:
:class:`~.statics.Load` whose downward part is a dead weight, added as a small box at the load point.

Returns ``(scene, layout, lift)``: ``layout[k] = (body index, brick indices, local brick centres [m])``; with
ground regions the scene is lifted by ``lift`` metres so the tables stand on Newton's ground plane, which
becomes the floor parts fall onto.

functions.name: replay
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, broken: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = (), *, duration: float = 0.8, dt: float = 0.001, solver: str = 'xpbd', iterations: int = 16, frames: int = 40, loads: Sequence = (), tol_mm: float = 2.0, joint: JointModel | None = None) -> Replay
functions.doc:
Simulate the build released at rest with ``broken`` joints let go. ``loads`` (:class:`~.statics.Load`): a
downward load is a dead weight (a small box of that weight at the load point, falling with the part instead of
pushing it with a constant force); horizontal parts are constant forces with their moment. Returns brick poses at
``frames`` evenly spaced times; raises ``FloatingPointError`` if the solver diverges.

functions.name: harmonic_threshold
functions.sig: (n: int = 4, length_mm: float = 63.8, *, factors: Sequence[float] = (0.9, 0.95, 0.98, 1.0, 1.02, 1.05, 1.1), duration: float = 0.8, mu: float = 0.4, tol_mm: float = 1.0, solver: str = 'xpbd') -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Newton on the harmonic stack of ``n`` smooth blocks with every offset scaled by ``f``: does the top block
stay (closed form: stands for f <= 1, falls for f > 1)? One row per factor.

functions.name: cross_check
functions.sig: (goal, candidates: Sequence, *, max_n: int = 30, duration: float = 0.4, tol_mm: float = 2.0, dt: float = 0.00025, iterations: int = 32, seed: int = 0) -> dict
functions.doc:
Does Newton agree with the statics verdict? For up to ``max_n`` evaluated candidates (``.asm``, ``.ev``) whose
verdict Newton can judge with every stud joint intact (``stable``: nothing should move by more than ``tol_mm``;
``mechanism``: something should), replay them under the goal's loads. Joint failures are left out: Newton has no
clutch model, so it cannot confirm or refute them. The small default ``dt`` keeps XPBD's friction creep under
a sustained sideways load (about 3 mm in 0.6 s at dt = 1 ms on a 5 g tower pushed with 10 mN) below ``tol_mm``.
Returns the rows and the confusion counts.

functions.name: friction_creep
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, loads: Sequence, *, dts: Sequence[float] = (0.001, 0.00025), duration: float = 0.6, iterations: int = 32) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Largest displacement of a build that should hold still under ``loads``, for several time steps: a sustained
sideways load makes XPBD friction creep by an amount that shrinks with ``dt`` (a solver artefact).

children.summary: Rigid-body replay of a brick build with NVIDIA Newton (pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics).

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.fea
children.doc:
Linear-elastic finite elements on the voxelised build (Hex8 with incompatible modes, :mod:`solid_fem`).

The build becomes one solid: every occupied cell (one stud pitch by one plate height) is split into
``per_stud`` x ``per_stud`` x 1 hexahedra and neighbouring cells share nodes, whether or not a stud joint links
them. That is an upper bound on stiffness: joint compliance and the 0.2 mm gaps between side-by-side parts are not
modelled, so use it for load paths and stresses in the plastic, and :mod:`.statics` for whether joints hold.
The same mesh can be solved by CalculiX through ``SolidFEM.calculix`` when ``ccx`` is installed.

Units: millimetres, newtons, MPa. ``E_ABS_MPA`` is an assumed modulus for moulded ABS; set your own.

functions.name: voxel_mesh
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, per_stud: int = 2) -> VoxelModel
functions.doc: Hexahedral mesh of the occupied cells, ``per_stud`` elements across a stud pitch, one per plate height.

functions.name: solve
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, loads: Sequence = (), *, E: float = E_ABS_MPA, nu: float = NU_ABS, per_stud: int = 2, gravity: bool = True, supports: str = 'ground', fixed_nodes = None) -> FEAResult
functions.doc:
Static linear elasticity of the voxelised build under gravity and point ``loads`` (:class:`~.statics.Load`).

``supports``: ``"ground"`` clamps the bottom nodes over the ground regions; ``"simple"`` gives vertical support
on those nodes with one corner pinned and another on a roller (a simply supported beam); or pass
``fixed_nodes`` = {node: dofs}.

children.summary: Linear-elastic finite elements on the voxelised build (Hex8 with incompatible modes, solid_fem).

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.goals
children.doc:
Design goals for the self-modifying loop: each one scores a build with the statics check and says why it fails.

* :class:`CantileverGoal`: the longest stable overhang past a table edge with at most N parts.
* :class:`BridgeGoal`: span a gap between two tables and carry a point load at mid-span with the fewest parts.
* :class:`TowerGoal`: the tallest tower that survives a lateral push at its top, with at most N parts.

All three are scored by :mod:`.statics` (rigid parts, stud clutch, friction); a score is only given to a build that
passes, and every failure comes with the explanation of the statics result (which joint, or where the centre of
mass left its support).

classes.name: Goal
classes.sig: (joint: JointModel | None = None)
classes.doc:
Base class. ``evaluate`` returns an :class:`Evaluation` whose ``violation`` follows one scale for every goal:
invalid build >= 5, unsupported parts >= 2, goal-specific geometric miss (e.g. no deck) in [2, 3), fails under
its own weight in [1, 2), overloaded (carries itself but not the load) in [0, 1), feasible 0.

methods.name: objectives
methods.doc: Minimised objectives for NSGA-II selection (primary first).

methods.name: features
methods.doc: Goal-agnostic descriptors of a build, for surrogate models.

classes.name: CantileverGoal
classes.sig: (max_bricks: int = 10, joint: JointModel | None = None)
classes.doc:
Reach as far past a table edge as possible with at most ``max_bricks`` 1-wide parts, under gravity.

The table is the half-plane x < 0 (smooth, friction ``mu``); parts are joined by studs. The score is the reach
of the farthest part end past the edge [mm]. Reference values: one block reaches L / 2, unconnected blocks one
per level reach (L / 2) H_n (harmonic stacking); welded parts could reach about n L / 2.

classes.name: BridgeGoal

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.ldraw
children.doc:
LDraw interchange: write and read .ldr / .mpd files, and load real part shapes from the LDraw parts library.

LDraw (ldraw.org) is the open file format and parts library for interlocking-brick CAD; files written here open in
LDraw-compatible editors and renderers. Units are LDraw units (1 LDU = 0.4 mm) and the LDraw frame has -Y up:
a point (x, y, z) mm of this package is (x, -z, y) / 0.4 in LDraw. A rectangular brick or plate has its origin at
the centre of its top face (where the studs start) and its long side along LDraw X.

The parts library is distributed under CC BY 2.0 (LDraw.org Parts Library, attribution required). It is not
copied into this repository: :func:`fetch_parts_library` downloads ``complete.zip`` at run time into a cache
folder, and anything rendered from it must credit "LDraw.org Parts Library, CC BY 2.0".

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.parts
children.doc:
Interlocking toy bricks: nominal dimensions, the part catalogue, masses and colours.

Dimensions (millimetres)
------------------------
The grid follows the LDraw unit system (1 LDU = 0.4 mm): a stud pitch of 20 LDU (8.0 mm), a plate 8 LDU high
(3.2 mm), a brick 24 LDU high (9.6 mm, three plates), studs 12 LDU in diameter (4.8 mm) and 4 LDU high (1.6 mm),
as drawn by the LDraw ``stud.dat`` primitive (LDraw File Format Specification and parts library, ldraw.org).
A part is 0.2 mm narrower than its grid cell (0.1 mm per side) so neighbours do not touch; an n-stud long part is
``8 n - 0.2`` mm long. StableLego uses the same 7.8 mm unit width (``Brick_Unit_Length = 0.0078`` m in the
public configuration of Liu et al., 2024).

Masses
------
Brick masses are the values of the StableLego brick library (``lego_library.json`` in
github.com/intelligent-control-lab/StableLego, MIT licence; Liu, Deng, Wang and Liu, "StableLego: Stability
Analysis of Block Stacking Assembly", IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 9(11), 9383-9390, 2024,
doi:10.1109/LRA.2024.3414281). Parts without a published mass (plates, 2x3, 2x8 bricks) are estimated with a
two-term shell model fitted to those masses, ``m = a * studs + b * perimeter * height``
(:func:`fit_mass_model`); :func:`mass_model_residuals` reports how well it reproduces the published values.

Colours
-------
The colour codes are LDraw colour numbers (used only when writing .ldr files); the RGB values here are
approximate display colours chosen for rendering, not the LDraw ``LDConfig.ldr`` values.

classes.name: PartType
classes.doc:
A rectangular brick or plate: ``nx`` x ``ny`` studs, ``h`` plates high (3 = brick, 1 = plate).

``ldraw`` is the LDraw part file of the same shape, whose long side lies along the LDraw x axis.
``smooth=True`` is a stud-less block of the same footprint (a tile, or a test body with no clutch).

methods.name: size_mm
methods.doc: Outer size of the body (without studs) in millimetres.

classes.name: JointModel
classes.doc:
Strength of a stud joint and contact friction used by the statics check.

``clutch_n``: tensile capacity of one stud-tube contact [N]. The default 0.98 N is the friction capacity per
stud reported for the StableLego analysis (Liu et al., IEEE RA-L 2024) and reused by BrickGPT (Pun et al.,
arXiv:2505.05469, 2025). Neither
source publishes a measurement uncertainty, and the public StableLego code ships a configuration with a
different value, so ``clutch_band`` is an *assumed* range for sensitivity studies, not a measured one.
Real clutch varies with wear, mould, temperature and how far the parts were pressed together.

``mu``: Coulomb friction for smooth contacts (a table, stud-less blocks). 0.4 is an assumption for ABS on a
hard surface; set it from your own measurement.

``shear_n``: cap on the horizontal force through one stud [N]. ``None`` (default) leaves it unbounded, as in
the StableLego force model, where horizontal stud forces are free; no published value bounds it. Overlapping
layers then act like a truss (horizontal forces at different heights make a couple), which can be
optimistic for bridges and cantilevers: compare with a finite cap to see how much a result relies on it.

``edge_inset_mm``: contact (compression and friction) acts at least this far inside the edge of a contact
patch. Real part and table edges are rounded, and a build balanced exactly on an edge is in neutral
equilibrium (it tips in a dynamic simulation), so a small inset keeps the search away from knife-edge designs.
0.5 mm is an assumption; set 0 to compare with sharp-edged closed forms.
fields: source: str = '0.98 N per stud: StableLego (Liu et al., IEEE RA-L 9(11), 2024, doi:10.1109/LRA.2024.3414281); BrickGPT (Pun et al., arXiv:2505.05469, 2025)'

notes: list[str] = field(default_factory=lambda: ['tension only: a stud joint fails when its pull-out force exceeds clutch_n', 'shear and torsion at stud joints are carried by the stud geometry (unbounded unless shear_n is set)', 'compression is unlimited (ABS crushing is far above these loads)', 'rigid parts: no joint compliance, so the force distribution is the most favourable one (lower bound)', 'a single stud is a pivot about the vertical (no torsion)', 'contact acts at least edge_inset_mm inside a patch edge (rounded edges, no knife-edge balance)'])

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.search
children.doc:
The self-modifying loop: mutate a build, simulate every candidate, keep what the physics accepts.

Edits (all on the stud grid):

* ``add``: a new part on top of or under an existing one, overlapping it by at least one stud;
* ``remove``, ``move`` (shift by 1-3 studs or one part height), ``swap`` (another part, same anchor),
  ``rotate`` (non-planar goals) and ``recolour`` (cosmetic: it does not change the score);
* grammar rules that read the last evaluation: ``extend`` (a part past the farthest end, overlapping it),
  ``counterweight`` (a part on the far side of the support), ``brace`` (a part across the joint that failed) and
  ``widen`` (a part next to the base), and ``mirror`` (replace one half of the build by the reflection of the
  other about the goal's target line, for spans).

Two search strategies with the same budget of physics evaluations (duplicates are looked up, not re-simulated):

* :func:`evolve`: (mu + lambda) evolution with NSGA-II survivor selection and Deb's constraint handling
  (:meth:`EvolutionaryDesignOptimizer._nsga2_select`), objectives from the goal (e.g. reach and part count);
* :func:`surrogate_search`: the same edits and selection, but each generation proposes many more children than it
  can afford, a Gaussian-process surrogate (:class:`GaussianProcessSurrogate`) trained on every build simulated so
  far ranks them by an upper confidence bound, and only the best are simulated.

functions.name: mutate
functions.sig: (goal: Goal, asm: Assembly, rng, last: Evaluation | None = None, edit: str | None = None) -> tuple[Assembly, str]
functions.doc: One random edit (or ``edit``). Returns the new build and the edit name; the build may be invalid.

functions.name: repair
functions.sig: (goal: Goal, asm: Assembly) -> Assembly
functions.doc: Drop parts that overlap an earlier one or float, so most edits give a buildable candidate.

functions.name: evolve
functions.sig: (goal: Goal, budget: int = 200, *, seed: int = 0, mu: int = 10, lam: int = 10, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None) -> SearchResult
functions.doc: (mu + lambda) evolution of builds with NSGA-II selection; ``budget`` physics evaluations.

functions.name: surrogate_search
functions.sig: (goal: Goal, budget: int = 200, *, seed: int = 0, mu: int = 10, lam: int = 10, pool: int = 8, kappa: float = 1.0, warmup: int = 20, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None) -> SearchResult
functions.doc:
Same loop, but each generation proposes ``pool * lam`` children, a GP surrogate trained on all simulated
builds ranks them by ``mean + kappa * std`` of a penalised score, and only the top ``lam`` are simulated.

functions.name: compare
functions.sig: (goal_factory: Callable[[], Goal], *, budget: int = 200, seeds = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4), strategies = ('evolution', 'surrogate'), progress = None, surrogate_kw: dict | None = None, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc:
Run every strategy with every seed at the same evaluation budget. ``kw`` (mu, lam) go to both strategies,
``surrogate_kw`` (pool, kappa, warmup) to the surrogate one. Returns the runs and a summary per strategy:
``best_median`` over all seeds with a seed that found no feasible build counted as the worst (nan when most
seeds found none), min and max over the feasible seeds, mean and standard deviation over the feasible seeds,
and the success rate.

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.statics
children.doc:
Static equilibrium of a brick build: contact forces, stud-joint utilisation, failure explanations.

Model (rigid parts, linear programme)
-------------------------------------
Every part is a rigid body loaded by its weight and by external point loads. Every contact patch between two
parts (or a part and the ground) is the overlap rectangle of their faces and carries

* compression ``c >= 0`` at the four corners of the patch (so the resultant can sit anywhere inside it), the
  corners moved ``JointModel.edge_inset_mm`` inwards (rounded edges; no knife-edge balance),
* at a stud joint: a clutch tension ``0 <= t_s <= clutch`` at each stud centre (the stud pulling out of its tube)
  and a horizontal force at each stud (shear and torsion through the stud walls), free as in StableLego or capped
  by ``JointModel.shear_n``;
* at a smooth contact (a table, a stud-less block): Coulomb friction at each corner, ``|f_x|, |f_y| <= mu c``.

Equilibrium of forces and moments of each body gives six equations. Among all force distributions that satisfy
them, :func:`analyse` finds the one with the smallest peak stud utilisation ``u = max t_s / clutch`` (then the
smallest total tension). By the lower-bound theorem of plasticity, if some admissible distribution keeps every
stud within its capacity, a rigid-plastic structure stands, so ``u <= 1`` means "stands" under these
assumptions and ``1 / u`` is the factor on gravity it could carry. No admissible distribution at all, even with
unbreakable studs, means a mechanism: the build tips or slides (reported with the centre of mass and the support
polygon it left). The model is optimistic: real clutch is brittle and joints are compliant, so the actual force
distribution is not the most favourable one.

Units: millimetres, newtons, kilograms.

classes.name: Interface
classes.doc:
Contact patch between ``lower`` (``-1`` = ground) and ``upper`` at height ``z`` [mm].

``rect``: (x0, x1, y0, y1) [mm]. ``studs``: (k, 2) stud centres [mm]; empty = smooth contact.

methods.name: corners
methods.doc: Corners of the patch, moved ``inset`` mm inwards (to the centre line when the patch is narrower).

methods.name: from_boxes
methods.sig: (boxes: Sequence[tuple[Sequence[float], Sequence[float]]], masses: Sequence[float], *, ground_z: float = 0.0, ground_rects: Sequence[tuple[float, float, float, float]] | None = None, tol: float = 1e-06) -> Structure
methods.doc: Smooth boxes (no studs) with contacts found where a top face meets a bottom face.

methods.name: margin
methods.doc: Load factor on gravity the build can carry (1 / utilisation; inf when no stud is loaded).

functions.name: from_assembly
functions.sig: (asm, loads: Sequence[Load] = (), broken: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = ()) -> Structure
functions.doc:
The :class:`Structure` of an :class:`~pinneapple_design.bricks.assembly.Assembly` (cell-bounds boxes).

``broken``: (lower, upper) brick pairs whose stud joint has failed; they keep a smooth (friction) contact.

functions.name: analyse
functions.sig: (structure: Structure, joint: JointModel | None = None) -> StaticsResult
functions.doc: Equilibrium under gravity and ``structure.loads`` with the smallest peak stud utilisation.

functions.name: capacity
functions.sig: (structure: Structure, joint: JointModel | None = None, lam_max: float = 1000000.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Largest factor ``lam`` on ``structure.loads`` (gravity fixed) with every stud within its clutch and an
equilibrium that exists (0 when even gravity alone is not carried; ``lam_max`` when the loads are carried
without limit).

functions.name: convex_hull
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Counter-clockwise convex hull of 2-D points (Andrew's monotone chain).

functions.name: signed_distance_inside
functions.sig: (poly: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc: Distance from ``p`` to the boundary of the convex polygon ``poly`` (ccw): > 0 inside, < 0 outside.

functions.name: centre_of_pressure
functions.sig: (s: Structure, members: Sequence[int], z0: float) -> np.ndarray | None
functions.doc:
Where the resultant of the weights and loads on ``members`` crosses the plane ``z = z0`` (None if the
resultant does not point down).

functions.name: tipping_report
functions.sig: (s: Structure, joint: JointModel | None = None) -> dict | None
functions.doc:
The worst support polygon left by a centre of pressure, treating stud joints as unbreakable.

Cuts examined: the ground (per group of parts welded by studs) and every smooth contact that alone carries
the parts above it. Returns ``{"members", "interfaces", "point", "distance_mm", "message"}`` for the worst cut
(distance < 0: outside the polygon), or None when every centre of pressure is inside its support.

functions.name: analyse_assembly
functions.sig: (asm, loads: Sequence[Load] = (), joint: JointModel | None = None, broken: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = ()) -> StaticsResult
functions.doc: :func:`analyse` of an assembly (gravity + ``loads``), with the stud joints in ``broken`` released.

functions.name: progressive_failure
functions.sig: (asm, loads: Sequence[Load] = (), joint: JointModel | None = None, max_rounds: int = 50) -> list[FailureRound]
functions.doc:
Release the most utilised stud joints one round at a time until the build stands or becomes a mechanism.

Each round solves :func:`analyse`; on a joint failure, the critical joints (those at the peak utilisation) lose
their clutch and keep a friction contact. The last round tells how the build ends: ``stable`` (it found a new
equilibrium after some joints let go) or ``mechanism`` (it collapses; replay it with :mod:`.dynamics`).

functions.name: top_load
functions.sig: (asm, force: Sequence[float], *, at: Sequence[float] | None = None, label: str = 'load') -> Load
functions.doc:
A point load on the highest part covering ``at`` = (x, y) [mm] (default: the centre of the top part), applied
at the top face.

functions.name: single_stud_torsion
functions.sig: (asm, loads: Sequence[Load] = (), joint: JointModel | None = None, spread_mm: float = 1.5) -> dict
functions.doc:
Does a verdict rest on single-stud joints having no torsion capacity? A lone stud is a pivot about the
vertical in this model; re-solve with each single-stud joint given three contact points ``spread_mm`` apart
(a little torsion and shear moment) and report both statuses.

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.validation
children.doc:
Checks of the brick physics against closed forms, gathered into a trust report.

:func:`validate` runs the statics LP, the Newton replay and the voxel FEA on cases with known answers and returns
one row per check plus a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`. Disagreements are reported, not hidden:
at exactly the harmonic limit the closed form is neutral equilibrium while Newton's compliant contacts tip it.

functions.name: harmonic_limit_lp
functions.sig: (n: int = 6, L: float = 63.8, tol: float = 0.0001, joint: JointModel | None = None) -> float
functions.doc:
Largest factor on the harmonic offsets the LP still finds stable (bisection; closed form: 1 for sharp edges,
``joint.edge_inset_mm = 0``).

functions.name: validate
functions.sig: (*, newton: bool | None = None, fea: bool = True, joint: JointModel | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Run every closed-form check. ``newton``: include the Newton replay checks (default: when installed). The
closed forms have sharp edges, so the statics checks use ``joint`` with ``edge_inset_mm = 0``.

Returns ``{"rows": [...], "harmonic_newton": [...], "report": TrustReport}``.

children.summary: Checks of the brick physics against closed forms, gathered into a trust report.

children.name: pinneapple_design.bricks.visuals
children.doc:
Pictures of the loop: the evolution as a timeline, the twin3d web viewer, GIF/MP4 frames, Blender renders and
building instructions.

A :class:`Frame` is a list of placed bricks (pose, colour, optional stud utilisation) plus red markers on joints that
broke. :func:`evolution_timeline` builds the frames of a search: for each generation, its best build at rest
coloured by stud utilisation (the load path), then one rejected candidate of that generation replayed by Newton
after the joints the statics check says fail are released. The same frames go to

* :func:`timeline_scene` -> the twin3d three.js viewer (time slider, play, field = stud utilisation, captions),
* :func:`render_frames` / :func:`write_gif` / :func:`write_mp4` (software renderer, no GPU),
* and the final build to :func:`render_blender` / :func:`turntable_blender` (Cycles) and
  :func:`write_instructions` (step-by-step layers, part list, an LDraw file with steps).

functions.name: build_frame
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, values: Sequence[float] | None = None, **kw) -> Frame
functions.doc: A frame of ``asm`` at rest; ``values``: stud utilisation per brick (colours the bricks by load path).

functions.name: scenery
functions.sig: (asms: Sequence[Assembly], thickness: float = 80.0, margin: float = 48.0) -> list[tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]]
functions.doc:
Table blocks under the builds (their ground regions near the parts, or one block for unlimited ground), as
tall as the drop to the floor in :mod:`.dynamics` by default.

functions.name: utilisation
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, loads = (), joint = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Worst stud utilisation of each brick's joints (0 = no stud in tension, 1 = at the clutch limit).

functions.name: replay_frames
functions.sig: (asm: Assembly, *, loads = (), joint = None, frames: int = 14, duration: float = 0.6, caption: str = '', short: str = '', generation: int = 0) -> list[Frame]
functions.doc:
Progressive failure (statics) then a Newton replay with the failed joints released: one frame per sample,

children.doc:
A chip floorplan: a die divided into placement slots, blocks with power densities and leakage, and the nets
whose delay matters.

The default floorplan is illustrative (a 10 mm x 10 mm die, six blocks of a mobile SoC class with round-number
powers); it is not data for a real product. Units: SI unless the name says otherwise (``_mm``, ``_w``).

classes.name: Block
classes.doc:
``dynamic_w``: switching power; ``leakage_w``: leakage at ``t_ref_c``, scaling as
``exp(leak_beta (T - t_ref))`` (sub-threshold leakage roughly doubles every 30-40 K).

classes.name: Floorplan
classes.doc:
``slots``: (nx, ny) equal rectangles tiling the die; ``placement[i]`` is the slot of ``blocks[i]``
(``slot = ix * ny + iy``). ``nets``: (block a, block b, weight) of the critical nets, routed centre to centre with
Manhattan length.

methods.sig: (slot: int, nx: int, ny: int) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Cells of an (nx, ny) die grid that fall in a slot (cell centres).

functions.sig: () -> Floorplan
functions.doc:
10 mm x 10 mm die, 3 x 2 slots: two CPU clusters, a GPU, an NPU, the L3 cache and the I/O ring segment;
the critical nets join the CPUs to the cache and the GPU and NPU to the cache.

children.summary: A chip floorplan: a die divided into placement slots, blocks with power densities and leakage, and the nets whose delay matters.

children.name: pinneapple_design.chip.interconnect
children.doc:
Interconnect delay of critical nets: a driver, a distributed RC wire as an RC ladder and a load; the Elmore delay
(first moment of the impulse response) and a SPICE-like transient (modified nodal analysis, trapezoidal rule, the
default integration of SPICE) that checks it.

Wire capacitance per length: Sakurai and Tamaru, IEEE Trans Electron Devices 30:183 (1983),
``C / eps = 1.15 (w / h) + 2.80 (t / h)^0.222`` (a line over a ground plane). Resistance ``rho(T) / (w t)`` with
``rho(T) = rho_20 (1 + alpha (T - 20))``. The Elmore delay is an upper bound of the 50 % delay of an RC tree's step
response (Gupta, Tutuianu and Pileggi, IEEE TCAD 16:95, 1997) and equals the integral of ``1 - v(t) / Vdd``.

classes.name: WireSpec
classes.doc:
A global (upper) metal line: width, thickness, height over the plane below, copper, low-k dielectric; a driver
resistance and a load capacitance (receiver gate). Representative values, not a foundry's.

functions.doc: Total resistance (ohm) and capacitance (F) of a wire.

functions.sig: (r_wire: float, c_wire: float, *, r_driver: float, c_load: float, n: int = 50)
functions.doc:
Series resistances and node capacitances of driver + n-segment pi-free ladder (C of each segment lumped at
its far node) + load at the last node.

functions.sig: (R: np.ndarray, C: np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc: Elmore delay at the last node of a chain: ``sum_i R_i sum_{j >= i} C_j``.

functions.doc:
Step response of the chain by MNA and the trapezoidal rule. Node 0 is the driver output (behind R[0]); a node
without capacitance is solved algebraically. Returns the far-node voltage, its 50 % crossing and the first moment
``int (1 - v / vdd) dt``.

functions.doc: Elmore delay and its single-pole 50 % estimate ``ln 2 tau`` for a driver-wire-load net.

children.name: pinneapple_design.chip.power_grid
children.doc:
On-chip power grid: IR drop on a resistive mesh fed by C4 bumps, and electromigration of every strap segment
against Black's equation at the segment's temperature.

The grid is the top-metal mesh of straps at ``pitch`` in x and y (one node per crossing); a segment between two
nodes has ``R = rho(T) pitch / (width thickness)``. Vdd bumps at ``bump_pitch`` connect nodes to an ideal supply
through ``r_bump``. The load current of a node is the power of the area it serves divided by Vdd.

Electromigration (Black, IEEE Trans Electron Devices 16:338, 1969): ``MTTF = A J^-n exp(Ea / k T)``. The constant is
fixed by a reference condition (``j_ref`` at ``t_ref_c`` lasts ``mttf_ref_years``), a design-rule style statement
of the technology's EM limit; the defaults (1 MA/cm^2 at 105 C for 10 years, n = 2, Ea = 0.9 eV for copper) are
typical published values, not a foundry's rule.

methods.name: metal_fraction
methods.doc: Area fraction of the top metal used by the x and y straps.

functions.name: black_mttf_years
functions.sig: (j_a_m2, t_c, spec: GridSpec) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: MTTF of a segment at current density ``j`` and temperature ``t_c`` from the reference condition.

functions.name: mesh_drop
functions.sig: (load_a: np.ndarray, gx: np.ndarray, gy: np.ndarray, *, pads: np.ndarray | None = None, g_pad: float = np.inf, fixed: np.ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
IR drop (Vdd - V) of every node for node load currents ``load_a``: ``L d + G_pad d = I``, with ``fixed``
nodes held at zero drop (ideal supply) and ``pads`` connected to it through ``g_pad``.

functions.name: uniform_grid_closed_form
functions.sig: (n: int, g: float, i_node: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Exact drop of an (n x n) interior mesh with every node sinking ``i_node`` and the boundary ring at zero drop:
the discrete sine expansion of the five-point Laplacian (eigenvalues ``4 - 2 cos(p pi/(n+1)) - 2 cos(q pi/(n+1))``).

functions.doc:

children.name: pinneapple_design.chip.thermal
children.doc:
Die and package thermal model of a flip-chip: a 3-D compact conduction network (cell-centred finite volumes, the
assembler of :func:`pinneapple_condense.fv.assemble`) from the board, through the C4 layer, the die, the TIM and the
lid, to the heat sink, with the leakage-temperature feedback solved to its fixed point.

Assumptions (stated in every result): the lid and the heat sink have the die's footprint (no lateral spreading
beyond the die, a conservative choice); the heat sink is a uniform conductance ``1 / (R_sink A_die)`` on the lid
top; the board path is a uniform conductance on the substrate bottom; the sides are adiabatic; conductivities are
constant (silicon's falls by about 20 % from 25 to 100 C, not modelled); heat is generated on the die's active
(bottom, flip-chip) cell row.

classes.name: DieStack
classes.doc:
Layers bottom to top; ``active``: the layer whose bottom cell row generates the heat; ``contacts``: (lower,
upper, m^2 K/W) interface resistances; ``r_sink_k_w``: heat-sink resistance (lid top to ambient, K/W) and
``r_board_k_w``: substrate bottom to ambient through the board (K/W).
fields: assumptions: tuple[str, ...] = field(default=('lid and heat sink with the die footprint (no spreading beyond the die)', 'uniform heat-sink and board conductances', 'adiabatic sides', 'constant conductivities', "heat generated on the die's active (bottom, flip-chip) cell row"))

functions.name: default_stack
functions.sig: () -> DieStack
functions.doc:
Organic substrate, C4 bumps in underfill (effective k), 500 um silicon, 50 um TIM, 2 mm copper lid.
Representative room-temperature values (Incropera, Table A.1, for Si and Cu; datasheet ranges for the rest).

functions.name: solve_thermal
functions.sig: (fp: Floorplan, stack: DieStack | None = None, *, nx: int = 24, ny: int | None = None, placement = None, leakage: bool = True, tol: float = 1e-06, max_iter: int = 100, operator: _Operator | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Steady junction temperatures with the leakage of every cell at its own temperature (fixed point).

The fixed-point map ``T -> T_amb + K^-1 q(T)`` contracts when the loop gain ``max eig K^-1 diag(dq/dT)`` is
below one; the measured ratio of successive corrections estimates it, and a gain at or above one is thermal
runaway (no steady state).

functions.name: slot_responses
functions.sig: (fp: Floorplan, op: _Operator) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Junction-temperature rise (n_slots, nx, ny) per watt spread uniformly over each slot: by superposition any
placement's map (at fixed power) is a weighted sum of these, which makes the placement search cheap.

functions.name: stack_closed_form
functions.sig: (stack: DieStack, area_m2: float, power_w: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
1-D die stack under uniform power: the series resistances from the source plane (the centre of the active
cell row) up through the die, TIM, lid and sink, and down through the C4 layer, substrate and board, in parallel.
``T_j = T_amb + P R_up R_down / (R_up + R_down)``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.chip.workflow
children.doc:
The standard chip-design workflow (#1206): floorplan, die and package thermal with the leakage-temperature loop,
power-grid IR drop with electromigration, Elmore delay of the critical nets, a placement and power-grid design, and
a finer thermal model that re-verifies it.

1. **Floorplan** (:mod:`.floorplan`): blocks with dynamic and leakage power in placement slots, critical nets.
2. **Thermal** (:mod:`.thermal`): a 3-D conduction network of the die stack (board, C4, die, TIM, lid, heat sink)
   with the leakage of every cell at its own temperature, iterated to the fixed point; the loop gain is measured
   and a gain >= 1 is thermal runaway. Checks: the energy balance (sink + board heat = power) and the 1-D stack
   against its closed-form resistance network.
3. **Placement**: every assignment of blocks to slots screened by superposition of per-slot responses (exact for
   the linear model at fixed power), the critical-net delays as constraints; the best re-solved with the leakage
   loop.
4. **Power grid** (:mod:`.power_grid`): IR drop on the strap mesh with the block powers at their temperatures and the
   strap resistivity at the local temperature; electromigration against Black's equation; the least strap width that
   meets the IR-drop and lifetime limits, within the metal-area budget. Checked: the mesh solver against the exact
   discrete-sine solution of a uniform grid, and that grid's continuum limit.
5. **Interconnect** (:mod:`.interconnect`): Elmore delay of each critical net with the wire at its temperature;
   checked against a SPICE-like trapezoidal transient (first moment equal to Elmore, 50 % delay below it).
6. **Re-verification**: the chosen design with a finer thermal mesh (lateral and vertical refinement).
7. **Lithography**: printability of the critical layers is the ``litho.opc`` node of #1180 (bundled in the flow).

children.name: pinneapple_design.design_gate
children.doc:
Três tipos de exigência, checados numa ordem fixa, e o registro de quem rejeitou cada projeto (#172).

Um projeto gerado é aprovado ou recusado por exigências de naturezas diferentes, e tratá-las como uma pilha só é como
um projeto reprovado chega ao solver para depois ser jogado fora:

* **restrições duras** (espessura > 2 mm, massa < 50 kg, folga > 5 mm, T < Tmax): nunca podem ser violadas, e são
  decididas sobre a geometria — antes de qualquer corrida;
* **restrições de física** (conservação de massa e de energia, condições de contorno, simetria): só podem ser ditas
  sobre uma solução;
* **objetivos suaves** (arrasto, sustentação, massa, eficiência térmica): medidos e ordenados, nunca impostos.

A ordem é a mesma para todo projeto e é o tipo que a determina, não o chamador: ``geometry`` → ``mesh`` →
``convergence`` → ``physics`` → ``objectives``. Uma falha para o projeto naquela etapa e a etapa fica registrada, com
a exigência que falhou.

>>> from pinneapple_design.design_gate import DesignGate, Requirement
>>> gate = DesignGate([Requirement.hard("thickness_mm >= 2.0", name="espessura"),
...                    Requirement.objective("cd", sense="min")])
>>> d = gate.evaluate({"thickness_mm": 1.4, "cd": 0.011}, run=lambda design: {"cd": 0.011})
>>> d.status, d.rejected_by
('rejected', 'geometry')

``run`` (o solver) só é chamado quando a geometria passa: é o que o aceite pede literalmente — um projeto que viola
uma restrição dura é recusado antes de qualquer corrida —, e ``DesignDecision.ran`` registra se ele chegou a rodar.

classes.name: Requirement
classes.doc:
Uma exigência, com o tipo e a etapa que o tipo permite.

``condition`` é uma expressão sobre os números do projeto (a mesma gramática das restrições do auditor de
dataset: ``"thickness_mm >= 2"``, ``"mass_kg <= 50"``, ``"clearance_mm > 5"``) ou ``func(values)`` para o que
não cabe numa expressão (a física medida, um objetivo que vem do solver). ``why`` guarda de onde a exigência
veio — a correção que a criou, a cláusula de projeto — porque uma regra sem procedência é a primeira a ser
ignorada.

children.name: pinneapple_design.design_optimizer
pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.adjoint
children.doc:
Continuous adjoint-based shape optimization for aerodynamic and thermal design.

Computes sensitivity dJ/d(shape) using the continuous adjoint method via
PyTorch autograd.  Supports objectives: drag, lift, heat flux, pressure drop.

Theory
------
Given primal PDE residual R(u, s) = 0 and objective J(u, s):

    dJ/ds = dJ/ds|_u  -  lambda^T  *  dR/ds

where lambda solves the *adjoint equation*:

    (dR/du)^T  lambda  =  (dJ/du)^T

In the discrete-PDE / PINN setting we use automatic differentiation to
evaluate all Jacobian-vector products without explicitly forming the Jacobians.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.adjoint import (
        ShapeParametrization, ContinuousAdjointSolver, naca_parametric
    )

    shape = ShapeParametrization(naca_parametric(t_c=0.12))
    solver = ContinuousAdjointSolver(pinn_model, pde_residual, objective_fn)
    result = solver.optimize(shape, x_col, n_steps=200, lr=1e-2)
    print(result["best_objective"])

classes.name: ShapeParametrization
classes.sig: (control_points: torch.Tensor, device: str = 'cpu') -> None
classes.doc:
Parametric shape representation for gradient-based optimisation.

Supports FFD (Free-Form Deformation) control points, Bezier curves, and
NACA 4-digit family parameter variations.

Parameters
----------
control_points:
    Initial control-point coordinates, shape ``(n_ctrl, 2)`` (2-D) or
    ``(n_ctrl, 3)`` (3-D).
device:
    Torch device to place the parameter on.

methods.name: deform_mesh
methods.doc: Apply a simple FFD-style deformation to *mesh_points*.

methods.name: to_boundary_coordinates
methods.doc: Return control points re-normalised to [-1, 1] chord coordinates.

methods.name: parameters
methods.doc: Return a list of trainable parameters for use with an optimiser.

classes.name: ContinuousAdjointSolver
classes.sig: (primal_model: nn.Module, pde_residual_fn: Callable, objective_fn: Callable) -> None
classes.doc:
Continuous adjoint solver using automatic differentiation.

Given:
- **Forward model** – a PINN solving the primal PDE: ``u = model(x)``
- **Objective**     – scalar ``J(u, x_col)``
- **PDE residual**  – ``R(u, x_col) ≈ 0``

``compute_adjoint`` solves the adjoint equation

    (dR/du)^T lambda = dJ/du

with a matrix-free Krylov (GMRES) solve driven by
``torch.autograd.grad`` Jacobian-vector products -- useful when ``u``
is the solution of a primal solve that is *not* differentiated through
directly (e.g. a black-box CFD solver).

``shape_sensitivity`` (used by ``optimize``) does **not** go through
the adjoint equation at all: in this module ``u = model(x_deformed(s))``
is a direct, fully differentiable forward pass, so ``dJ/ds`` is simply
the total derivative obtained by backpropagating through
``deform_mesh`` and the model -- exact, and cheaper than any adjoint
correction.

Parameters
----------
primal_model:
    Trained (or being trained) PINN, callable ``(x) -> u``.
pde_residual_fn:
    Callable ``(model, x_col) -> residual_tensor``.  The residual should
    be differentiable with respect to the shape parameters embedded in
    *x_col* or *model*.
objective_fn:
    Callable ``(model, x_col) -> scalar_tensor``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.airfoil_drag
children.doc:
Worked design study: cut the profile drag of a NACA 4-digit section while holding its lift, with the
surrogate-driven gradient loop of this package.

Ground truth: :mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.thin_airfoil` (thin-airfoil lift of the camber line, Hoerner
profile drag of the thickness). A :class:`~.surrogate.PhysicsSurrogate` MLP learns (camber m, thickness t/c) ->
(Cl, Cd) from samples of that ground truth; :class:`~.pipeline.DesignOptLoop` runs Adam steps on the design through
the surrogate with a :class:`~.objective.CompositeObjective` (drag + weight * (Cl - Cl_baseline)^2) and a
:class:`~.constraints.BoxConstraint` (0-6 % camber, 8-18 % thickness). Every iterate is re-evaluated with the
closed-form physics, so the reported drag and lift are the physics' numbers, not the surrogate's belief.

Training detail that matters: Cl ~ O(1) and Cd ~ O(1e-2). A plain MSE on both is dominated by Cl, and the surrogate
can learn the wrong sign of dCd/d(t/c) at the baseline, which stalls the optimiser. The targets are therefore
normalised per channel (training-set mean and standard deviation) and the trained network is composed with a fixed
affine un-normalisation layer, so the optimiser sees physical units and exact gradients through it.

Scope: the ground truth has no thickness effect on lift and no camber effect on drag (see the physics module), so the
optimum found is "thinnest section allowed, camber nudged to keep Cl"; a panel method or RANS would trade these off.

``run_design_optimization(seed=...)`` is fully reproducible for a given seed; ``seed=None`` draws a fresh one.

children.name: pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.cantilever
children.doc:
A tapered cantilever under a tip load: a gmsh-parametrized geometry solved by plane-stress finite elements, the
same quantities from beam theory, and the CAD (STEP) of a design. It is the reference problem of the design
optimisation workflow (:mod:`.workflow`, #1188): minimum mass under a stress and a deflection limit has a known
optimum through beam theory.

    from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.cantilever import tapered_cantilever, tapered_cantilever_beam
    tapered_cantilever(h_root=0.12, h_tip=0.04, n_through=4)      # FEM on a gmsh mesh
    tapered_cantilever_beam(h_root=0.12, h_tip=0.04)              # Euler-Bernoulli + Timoshenko shear

Geometry: a beam of length ``length`` along x, clamped at x = 0, depth varying linearly from ``h_root`` to ``h_tip``
(symmetric about y = 0), out-of-plane width ``thickness``. Load: ``load`` [N] downwards, as a uniform shear traction
on the tip edge.

Mesh: gmsh transfinite (structured) triangles, ``n_through`` across the depth and ``n_along`` along the length. The
node counts do not depend on the design, so the mesh moves with the geometry and every output is a smooth function
of the dimensions (finite-difference gradients work); ``n_through`` is the fidelity (refine it to re-verify).

Outputs: ``mass_kg``; ``stress_max_Pa``, the largest bending (fibre) stress |sigma_xx| at the top and bottom surfaces
over the stations ``x_from <= x <= 0.9 length``; ``tip_deflection_m``, the mean downward displacement of the tip
edge. On the FEM, the fibre stress at a station comes from a least-squares fit ``sigma_xx = a + b x + c y + d x y``
over the elements whose centroid is within one element length of the station (bending stress is linear in y),
evaluated at the station's surfaces.

Assumptions (stated in the outputs): linear elasticity, plane stress, small displacements; the stations start at
``x_from`` (0.1 length by default) because the stress at a fully clamped edge is singular in plane elasticity
(Saint-Venant zone); the fibre stress is sigma_xx, not the stress along the inclined surface (they differ by a
factor 1 + tan^2(alpha), 0.6 % at a taper angle of 4.4 degrees). References: Timoshenko & Gere, *Mechanics of
Materials* (1997), ch. 5 and 9 (bending stress, deflection by integration); Cowper (1966), J. Appl. Mech. 33:335
(shear coefficient 10(1+nu)/(12+11nu) of a rectangle).

children.name: pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.compare
children.doc:
Compare optimisation methods on the same problem and the same evaluation budget.

Every method gets the same evaluator, the same budget and the same seeds. The convergence metric is the
hypervolume of the feasible, realisable designs found so far, with the objectives normalised between the ideal and
nadir points of the feasible designs found by *all* runs (reference point 1.1 per axis), so the numbers are
comparable across methods. A run "converged" when its hypervolume grew by less than ``tol`` (relative) over the last
quarter of the evaluations it made; ``evals_to_95`` is the number of evaluations it needed to reach 95 % of the best
final hypervolume of any run.

methods.name: table
methods.doc: One row per method (seeds aggregated: mean final hypervolume, worst/best, total wall time).

methods.name: union
methods.doc:
All evaluations of all runs in one record, and the run (``"<method>#<seed>"``) of each row; its
:meth:`~.study.Evaluations.pareto` is the best front any method found, each member labelled by who found it.

methods.name: union_result
methods.doc:
The comparison as one :class:`~.methods.OptimizationResult` (method ``"comparison: <methods>"``, the
first seed, every run's evaluations and the summed budget and wall time), e.g. for
:func:`~.report.study_result`. None when no run produced evaluations.

methods.name: fronts
methods.doc:
Pareto front of each method's run with ``seed`` (default: the first seed), in the objectives' own units
and senses (one list of objective values per member).

functions.name: compare_methods
functions.sig: (problem: DesignProblem, methods: Sequence[str], *, budget: int = 300, seeds: Sequence[int] = (0,), tol: float = 0.01, options: dict[str, dict] | None = None, progress = None) -> MethodComparison
functions.doc:
Run every method in ``methods`` once per seed with ``budget`` evaluations and tabulate the outcome.

``progress(done, total)`` counts runs (fractional while a run is going).
