children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.threaded_connection
children.doc:
Threaded connection geometry for rotary coupling PINN simulations.

Generates 2D axisymmetric (r, z) meshes of rotary threaded connections
using gmsh. The mesh is compatible with FEniCS/dolfinx and the
SolidMechanicsPipeline.

Supported connections
---------------------
  TC50  — large-diameter coupling, 4 TPI, taper 1:16
  TC46  — medium-diameter coupling, 4 TPI, taper 1:16
  TC38  — standard coupling, 4 TPI, taper 1:16
  Custom — any V-thread via ThreadProfile

Thread profile (API V-0.038R)
------------------------------
  Pitch     p = 25.4 / TPI   mm
  Taper     T = 1:16  →  Δr/Δz = 1/32 per side
  Height    h_total = 0.8660 · p
  Clearance c = 0.038 · p     (root flat)
  Crest cut = 0.038 · p

In the 2D (r, z) cross-section the thread appears as a sawtooth on the
inner/outer cylindrical surfaces of the connection.

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.threaded_connection import TC50Geometry

    geom = TC50Geometry(body="BOX")
    mesh_path = geom.generate_mesh(output="mesh_tc50_box.msh", lc=0.5)
    # → Mesh2D / .msh file ready for FEniCS or point sampling

classes.name: ThreadedConnectionMesher
classes.sig: (spec: ConnectionSpec, lc: float = 1.0, lc_thread: Optional[float] = None)
classes.doc:
Generates a 2D axisymmetric mesh of an API threaded connection using gmsh.

The mesh represents the (r, z) cross-section. Boundary regions are tagged:
  - "bore"         : inner cylindrical surface (r = r_bore)
  - "outer"        : outer cylindrical surface (r = r_outer)
  - "nose"         : z = z_min face (thread start, fixed nose)
  - "shoulder_top" : z = z_max face (make-up shoulder / top)
  - "thread_flank" : threaded surface (sawtooth profile)

Parameters
----------
spec : ConnectionSpec
    Geometry parameters for the connection body.
lc : float
    Characteristic mesh size (mm). Smaller = finer.
lc_thread : float
    Finer mesh size at thread root/crest (default = lc / 3).

functions.name: build_thread_polygon
functions.sig: (spec: ConnectionSpec, n_threads: Optional[int] = None) -> List[Tuple[float, float]]
functions.doc:
Builds the (r, z) polygon that describes the threaded surface profile.

The result is a list of (r, z) points forming the sawtooth thread profile
on the relevant cylindrical surface:
  BOX: inner surface (r = r_bore side) → threads cut INTO the box bore
  PIN: outer surface (r = r_outer side) → threads on pin outer diameter

The taper is applied: the thread reference diameter increases from
z_thread_start toward z_thread_end at rate `taper` (radial/axial).

Returns ordered (r, z) vertices for the threaded profile segment.
The full boundary polygon is assembled by the mesh builder.

mesh_path = geom.generate("mesh_tc50_box.msh")

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.io.iges
children.doc:
IGES file import utilities.

This module provides optional IGES -> mesh conversion.

Preferred backend:
  - gmsh (Python API), which embeds an OpenCASCADE (OCC) kernel capable of
    reading IGES (.iges/.igs) files via the same ``model.occ.importShapes``
    entry point used for STEP in :mod:`pinneapple_design.geometry.io.step`.

This is an optional dependency. If not installed, functions raise a clear error.

Notes:
  - IGES, like STEP, is CAD (B-Rep / surface) data. For PINNs / operators we
    typically convert to a triangle mesh (surface) or a volume mesh (tetra)
    depending on the downstream solver/model.
  - IGES is an older, surface-oriented format: solids are frequently
    represented as (possibly imperfectly stitched) collections of trimmed
    surfaces rather than a single watertight B-Rep solid the way STEP AP203/
    AP214 files usually are. Volume meshing ("kind='volume'") can therefore
    fail on IGES files that STEP handles fine -- callers needing a solid mesh
    should prefer STEP when available and treat IGES as a surface-mesh source.
  - This module intentionally mirrors ``step.py``'s config/return shape so the
    two importers are interchangeable from a caller's point of view.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh
pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh.generate
children.doc:
Unstructured mesh generation with gmsh: triangles in 2-D, tetrahedra (and prism layers at the walls) in 3-D, from
a parametric primitive or a geometry file, with the quality of every element.

    from pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh.generate import generate_mesh
    out = generate_mesh("cylinder", [0.5, 2.0], h=0.1, out_dir="mesh_out")
    out["n_elements"], out["sicn_min"], out["volume"]          # tetrahedra, worst element, 1.567 m3 (pi r^2 H)
    out["files"]                                              # mesh.msh, mesh.vtu, quality.glb, quality.json

Geometry (lengths in metres):

=============  =======================  =========================================================================
``box``        ``[lx, ly, lz]``         corner at the origin
``cylinder``   ``[radius, height]``     base centred at the origin, axis +z
``sphere``     ``[radius]``             centred at the origin
``rectangle``  ``[lx, ly]``             2-D, corner at the origin
``disk``       ``[radius]``             2-D, centred at the origin
a file         ``.stl``                 a closed surface (open or non-manifold edges are refused); meshed with
                                        :func:`.mesher_3d.mesh_from_surface`
               ``.step .stp .iges``     through OpenCASCADE (gmsh's OCC kernel); ``scale`` converts to metres
=============  =======================  =========================================================================

``h`` is the target element size; ``refine`` adds balls of smaller size (``{"center", "radius", "h"}``) with a smooth
transition back to ``h``; ``boundary_layer`` (``{"first_layer", "n_layers", "growth"}``) adds layers at the walls:
prisms extruded inward from the surface in 3-D, a layer of triangles along the boundary in 2-D.

Quality comes from gmsh (``minSICN``: signed inverse condition number, 1 for the ideal element, <= 0 inverted;
``gamma``: inscribed / circumscribed radius, normalised to 1 for the ideal element) and from
:func:`pinneapple_data.cae.quality.element_metrics` (``aspect_ratio`` = longest / shortest edge of each element).
The view is :func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.fieldview.field_view` with those three fields per element.

functions.name: estimate_elements
functions.sig: (dim: int, measure: float, boundary: float, h: float, refine: list[dict[str, Any]], boundary_layer: dict[str, Any] | None) -> float
functions.doc: Elements gmsh will make, from the measured densities (an upper estimate within about 30 %).

functions.name: generate_mesh
functions.sig: (geometry: str = 'box', dimensions: list[float] | None = None, h: float = 0.25, scale: float = 1.0, refine: list[dict[str, Any]] | None = None, boundary_layer: dict[str, Any] | None = None, out_dir: str | None = None, origin: list[float] | None = None, max_input_mb: float | None = None, max_elements: int = MAX_ELEMENTS) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Mesh a primitive or a geometry file with gmsh and rate every element.

Parameters
----------
geometry : str
    ``box``, ``cylinder``, ``sphere``, ``rectangle`` or ``disk``, or the path of an ``.stl``, ``.step``,
    ``.stp``, ``.iges`` or ``.igs`` file
dimensions : list[float]
    size of the primitive [m]: box [lx, ly, lz], cylinder [radius, height], sphere [radius], rectangle
    [lx, ly], disk [radius] (default: a unit box, 0.5 m radii)
h : float
    target element size [m]
scale : float
    factor from the file's length unit to metres (1e-3 for millimetres) [-]
refine : list[dict]
    balls of smaller elements, ``{"center": [x, y, z], "radius": r, "h": h_local}`` (metres)
boundary_layer : dict
    ``{"first_layer": m, "n_layers": int, "growth": ratio}``: prism layers at the walls (3-D) or triangle
    layers along the boundary (2-D)
out_dir : str
    folder for mesh.msh, mesh.vtu, quality.glb and quality.json (nothing is written without it)
origin : list[float]
    where the primitive's reference point (the corner of a box or rectangle, the centre of a sphere or disk, the
    base centre of a cylinder) goes [m] (default: the origin)
max_input_mb : float
    largest geometry file accepted, checked before the file is opened [MB] (default:
    PINNEAPPLE_MESH_MAX_INPUT_MB, else 100)
max_elements : int
    refuse, before meshing, a mesh estimated above this many elements (from the volume or area over h^d, the
    refinement balls and the wall layers; files: their bounding box) [-]

Returns
-------
dim : int [-]
    dimension of the mesh
n_nodes : int [-]
    nodes
n_elements : int [-]
    elements of the mesh's dimension
element_counts : dict [-]
    elements per type
sicn_min : float [-]
    worst signed inverse condition number (1 ideal, <= 0 inverted)
sicn_mean : float [-]
    mean signed inverse condition number
gamma_min : float [-]
    worst inscribed / circumscribed radius ratio (1 ideal)
gamma_mean : float [-]
    mean gamma
aspect_ratio_max : float [-]
    largest longest-to-shortest edge ratio
aspect_ratio_mean : float [-]
    mean edge ratio
volume : float [m3]
    volume of the 3-D mesh (null in 2-D)
area : float [m2]
    area of the 2-D mesh, or of the 3-D boundary
h_min : float [m]
    shortest edge
h_mean : float [m]
    mean edge length
h_max : float [m]
    longest edge
files : dict
    paths of the written files
backend : str
    how the mesh was made

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh.mesher_3d
children.doc:
3D mesh generation from surfaces and SDFs.

Workflow
--------
1. Load or create a 3D surface mesh (STL/OBJ/SDF/primitives).
2. Clean it with ``ops.clean.clean_mesh``.
3. Generate a volume mesh (tetrahedral) with ``mesh_from_surface``.
4. Sample physics collocation points with ``sample_physics_points``.

Backends
--------
  gmsh      — high-quality tet mesh with boundary layer support (preferred)
  tetgen    — fast tet meshing via pyvista/tetgen
  trimesh   — surface only (no volume; used for sampling)
  open3d    — surface reconstruction from point clouds

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh.mesher_3d import (
        mesh_from_surface, mesh_from_sdf_3d,
        sample_physics_points, PhysicsPointCloud3D,
    )
    from pinneapple_design.geometry.core.mesh import MeshData

    # From a cleaned surface mesh
    vol_mesh = mesh_from_surface(surface_mesh)
    pts = sample_physics_points(surface_mesh, n_interior=10000, n_boundary=2000)
    pts.interior   # (N, 3) collocation points
    pts.boundary   # (M, 3) BC points

    # From an SDF
    vol_mesh = mesh_from_sdf_3d(my_sdf_fn, bounds_min=(-1,-1,-1), bounds_max=(1,1,1))

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh_collocator
children.doc:
MeshCollocator — 3D collocation point sampler for PINN training.

Bridges the gap between 3D geometry (MeshData from step_to_mesh / STL import)
and PINN training by producing interior collocation points (for PDE residuals)
and surface boundary points (for BC enforcement).

Supports:
- Bounding-box interior sampling (fast, no extra deps)
- Convex-hull interior sampling via scipy (good for convex bodies)
- Trimesh ray-casting for watertight meshes (precise, requires trimesh)
- Hollow geometry: outer mesh minus inner mesh (e.g. pipe, heat sink)

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_design.geometry.mesh_collocator import MeshCollocator, MeshCollocatorConfig
>>> from pinneapple_design.geometry.io.step import step_to_mesh, StepImportConfig
>>> mesh = step_to_mesh("part.step", cfg=StepImportConfig(kind="surface"))
>>> col = MeshCollocator(mesh)
>>> batch = col.sample()
>>> batch.X_interior.shape   # (5000, 3)
>>> batch.X_boundary.shape   # (2000, 3)

classes.name: MeshCollocatorConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for MeshCollocator.

Parameters
----------
n_interior : int
    Number of interior collocation points to sample.
n_boundary : int
    Number of surface / boundary collocation points.
domain : str
    Interior sampling strategy:
    - ``"bbox"`` — uniform inside bounding box (fast, coarse).
    - ``"convex_hull"`` — rejection sampling with scipy ConvexHull test.
    - ``"trimesh"`` — ray-cast inside test (requires *trimesh*; precise).
boundary_mode : str
    - ``"surface"`` — sample uniformly on triangle surface (area-weighted).
    - ``"bbox_planes"`` — sample on the 6 bounding-box faces.
hollow : bool
    If True, sample the *fluid* domain: inside the outer mesh but outside
    the inner mesh.  Pass ``inner_mesh`` to :class:`MeshCollocator`.
seed : int, optional
    Random seed for reproducibility.
max_rejection_tries : int
    Maximum rejection-sampling rounds before giving up and falling back to
    bbox.  Each round oversamples by 2×.

    Outward surface normals at boundary points (if available).

    Named boundary groups mapping name → indices into ``X_boundary``.
    Populated when ``boundary_mode="bbox_planes"``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.ops
pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.clean
children.doc:
Comprehensive 3D mesh cleaning pipeline.

Provides a layered cleaning pipeline that goes well beyond the basic
``repair_mesh`` (duplicate removal / degenerate face removal).  Every step is
optional so callers can pick only what they need.

Pipeline order (default)
------------------------
1. merge_vertices         — weld vertices within a tolerance
2. remove_degenerate      — zero-area triangles
3. remove_duplicates      — duplicate faces
4. remove_unreferenced    — vertices not used by any face
5. fix_normals            — make face normals consistently outward
6. fill_holes             — attempt to close small boundary loops
7. remove_self_intersect  — detect and remove self-intersecting faces (pymeshlab)
8. smooth                 — Laplacian or Taubin smoothing
9. remove_outliers        — statistical outlier vertex removal
10. keep_largest           — discard all but the largest connected component
11. ensure_watertight      — final watertight check, trim if needed
12. decimate              — reduce polygon count to target face count

All heavy-lifting uses trimesh (always required) and pymeshlab (optional).
open3d is used opportunistically for outlier removal and smoothing.

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.clean import clean_mesh, CleanMeshConfig
    from pinneapple_design.geometry.core.mesh import MeshData

    cfg = CleanMeshConfig(smooth=True, smooth_iterations=5, keep_largest=True)
    cleaned = clean_mesh(mesh, config=cfg)
    print(cleaned.quality_report())

classes.doc: Full configuration for the clean_mesh pipeline.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.curvature
children.doc:
Discrete differential geometry on triangle surface meshes (NumPy/SciPy).

Real curvature for the geometry pipeline (``features.compute_curvature_proxy``
is only a normal-variation proxy): useful as a CAD/mesh quality feature, as a
geometry descriptor for surrogate models (curvature drives boundary-layer
behaviour and stress concentration) and for OOD checks on new shapes.

Operators -- Meyer, Desbrun, Schroeder & Barr (2003), "Discrete
differential-geometry operators for triangulated 2-manifolds":

- :func:`mixed_areas`          Voronoi areas, with the mixed-area rule for
                               obtuse triangles (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 4)
- :func:`cotan_laplacian`      cotangent stiffness matrix ``C`` (Eq. 8);
                               Laplace-Beltrami ``Delta f = M^{-1} C f``
- :func:`gaussian_curvature`   angle defect / area (Eq. 9); boundary vertices
                               use ``pi`` as the full angle (geodesic-curvature
                               term) or are reported as NaN
- :func:`mean_curvature`       ``Delta x = -2 H n`` (Eq. 7); sign from the
                               area-weighted vertex normal
- :func:`principal_curvatures` ``k1,2 = H +- sqrt(max(H^2 - K, 0))``

Harvest note: the operator choice (mixed Voronoi areas, angle defect, the
discrete Gauss-Bonnet identity as the acceptance test) follows NVIDIA
PhysicsNeMo's ``physicsnemo.mesh.curvature`` (Apache-2.0), studied for this
module; this is an independent NumPy implementation, not a copy of that
PyTorch code. See ``docs/dev/rea_harvest/ledger.json``.

functions.name: boundary_vertices
functions.sig: (mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Boolean mask of vertices on a boundary edge (edge used by one face).

functions.name: euler_characteristic
functions.sig: (mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None) -> int

functions.name: mixed_areas
functions.sig: (mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Per-vertex mixed Voronoi area; the areas sum to the surface area.

functions.name: cotan_laplacian
functions.sig: (mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None) -> sparse.csr_matrix
functions.doc:
Symmetric cotangent matrix ``C`` with ``C_ij = (cot a_ij + cot b_ij)/2``
off the diagonal and ``C_ii = -sum_j C_ij``; ``(C f)_i`` is the Laplacian
of ``f`` integrated over vertex i's mixed area (Eq. 8), so the pointwise
Laplace-Beltrami is ``(C f)_i / A_i``.

functions.name: laplace_beltrami
functions.sig: (f: np.ndarray, mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Pointwise Laplace-Beltrami of a vertex field ``f`` (n,) or (n, d).

functions.name: gaussian_curvature
functions.sig: (mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None, *, boundary: str = 'geodesic') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Angle-defect Gaussian curvature per vertex.

``boundary="geodesic"`` uses ``pi - sum(angles)`` at boundary vertices,
so ``sum(K * area)`` obeys discrete Gauss-Bonnet ``2 pi chi`` for surfaces
with boundary too; ``boundary="nan"`` marks them NaN instead.

functions.name: mean_curvature
functions.sig: (mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None, *, signed: bool = True, boundary: str = 'nan') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Mean curvature ``H`` per vertex from ``Delta x = -2 H n``.

Signed with respect to the outward vertex normal implied by the face
winding (a counter-clockwise-outward sphere has ``H = +1/R``). Boundary
vertices are NaN by default (the operator is one-sided there).

functions.name: principal_curvatures
functions.sig: (mesh_or_vertices: Any, faces: np.ndarray | None = None) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.lbm_bridge
children.doc:
Bridge from a surface mesh (STL / trimesh) to a boolean LBM obstacle mask.

Composes three pieces of existing geometry infrastructure that previously had
no glue between them:

  * mesh loading -- ``TrimeshBridge`` / ``pinneapple_design.geometry.io.stl``
    (returns :class:`~pinneapple_design.geometry.core.mesh.MeshData`, itself
    a thin numpy wrapper the caller can build a raw ``trimesh.Trimesh`` from)
  * point-in-mesh / voxel-grid machinery --
    :mod:`pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.voxelize` (``VoxelGrid``,
    ``voxelize_sdf``)
  * the angle-of-attack rotation convention already used for the 2D NACA
    obstacle path -- ``airfoil_naca_mask`` in
    ``pinneapple_simulation/numerical_solvers/lbm.py``

into "load an STL -> get a boolean 3D occupancy grid I can hand to an LBM
solver as its solid mask", with the same AoA sign meaning a caller would
already know from the 2D NACA path.

functions.name: mesh_to_obstacle_mask
functions.sig: (mesh, bounds: Dict[str, Tuple[float, float]], resolution: Union[int, Tuple[int, int, int]], *, aoa_deg: float = 0.0, rotation_axis: str = 'y', oracle_supersample: int = 2, device: torch.device = torch.device('cpu')) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Voxelize a surface mesh into a boolean 3D LBM obstacle/solid mask.

Parameters
----------
mesh : trimesh.Trimesh | MeshData | mesh-like
    Surface mesh, e.g. from ``TrimeshBridge().load(path)`` or
    ``pinneapple_design.geometry.io.stl.load_stl(path)`` (both return
    :class:`MeshData`), or a raw ``trimesh.Trimesh``.
bounds : {"x": (x0, x1), "y": (y0, y1), "z": (z0, z1)}
    World-space extent of the LBM domain to voxelize over (same format
    as :func:`pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.voxelize.voxelize_sdf`).
resolution : int | (nx, ny, nz)
    Output grid resolution (isotropic if a single int).
aoa_deg : float
    Angle of attack in degrees. The mesh is rotated by this amount about
    its own centroid, about ``rotation_axis``, before voxelizing -- see
    :func:`_aoa_rotation_matrix` for the exact sign/axis convention
    (mirrors ``airfoil_naca_mask`` in
    ``pinneapple_simulation/numerical_solvers/lbm.py``).
rotation_axis : {"x", "y", "z"}
    Axis to rotate about. Default "y" (pitch about the spanwise axis,
    i.e. rotate in the streamwise/x - vertical/z plane) -- the natural
    3D generalization of the 2D NACA path's (x, y) rotation.
oracle_supersample : int
    The internal point-in-mesh oracle (see implementation note below)
    is built at a pitch finer than the output grid's own voxel size by
    this factor, to reduce aliasing at the mesh surface. Default 2.
device : torch.device
    Device for the returned/intermediate grid computation.

Returns
-------
np.ndarray of shape ``resolution`` (or the (nx,ny,nz) tuple), dtype
bool. ``True`` = solid/occupied (inside the mesh) -- directly usable as
an LBM ``obstacle_mask`` (matching the ``obstacle_mask: bool tensor``
convention documented on ``LBMSolver``/``LBMSolver3D`` in
``pinneapple_simulation/numerical_solvers/lbm.py``, modulo needing a
``torch.from_numpy(...)`` there since this module stays numpy-only).

Implementation note -- why ``voxelize_sdf`` and not ``voxelize_pointcloud``
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Both were viable per the audit: ``voxelize_pointcloud`` could rasterize
points sampled on the mesh *surface*, and ``voxelize_sdf`` evaluates an
arbitrary inside/outside predicate on a dense grid of cell-center query
points. ``voxelize_sdf`` was chosen because it maps directly onto "solid
occupancy volume" semantics: a surface point cloud only rasterizes a
thin shell (it says nothing about the interior) and would need its own
separate flood-fill step to become a solid mask, duplicating exactly
what ``voxelize_sdf`` already gets for free from evaluating a
containment predicate at every grid cell.

That still leaves "what containment predicate": the obvious choice,
``trimesh.Trimesh.contains()`` (ray casting), requires an rtree/pyembree
broad-phase index that is NOT guaranteed to be installed -- confirmed by
actually calling it against a real trimesh 5.1.0 install in this repo's
own ``.venv``, which raises ``ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
'rtree'``, not by reading trimesh's docs. Instead this uses
``trimesh.Trimesh.voxelized(pitch).fill()`` (the same
voxel-occupancy approach already used elsewhere in this repo, see
``stl_domain_batch_builder._inside_voxel_occupancy``), which rasterizes
the surface and flood-fills the interior via scipy (already a hard
dependency elsewhere in this package, e.g. ``MeshCollocator``'s
``ConvexHull`` path) without touching the ray/rtree path at all. That
gives a plain boolean ``is_filled(points)`` oracle, which is then wired
into ``voxelize_sdf`` as a signed-distance-like function (``-1`` inside,
``+1`` outside, thresholded at 0) so the final grid still goes through
this module's shared ``VoxelGrid`` machinery instead of reimplementing
grid math here.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.meshfree
children.doc:
Meshfree geometry utilities.

Provides geometry-focused meshfree operations that complement
pinneapple_geom's mesh and point-cloud tooling:

  RBFInterpolator
      Scattered field interpolation / transfer between point clouds.
      Useful for mapping CFD results to PINN collocation grids, upsampling
      scalar/vector fields, or generating smooth reference data.

  ImplicitSurfaceRBF
      Point cloud + normals -> continuous SDF approximation.
      Reconstructs a signed distance function from scattered boundary samples
      without requiring an explicit mesh, enabling direct use as a PINN domain.

For *PDE solving* via meshfree methods (Kansa RBF collocation, MLS collocation)
see ``pinneapple_solvers.meshfree``.

classes.name: RBFInterpolator
classes.sig: (kernel: str = 'gaussian', eps: float = 1.0, reg: float = 1e-10) -> None
classes.doc:
Scattered data interpolation via Radial Basis Functions.

Fits a global RBF interpolant to paired (source_pts, source_vals) and
evaluates it at arbitrary query points. Useful for:

- Transferring field data (velocity, pressure, temperature) from a CFD
  mesh to a PINN collocation grid.
- Upsampling scalar or vector fields on point clouds.
- Mapping simulation results onto a denser evaluation set.

This is a *pure interpolation* tool — it does not solve PDEs. For
meshfree PDE solving (Kansa method, MLS collocation) see
``pinneapple_solvers.meshfree.RBFCollocationSolver``.

Parameters
----------
kernel : "gaussian" | "multiquadric" | "imq" | "thin_plate"
    Radial basis function kernel.
eps : float
    Shape parameter controlling kernel width (not used for thin_plate).
reg : float
    Tikhonov regularisation added to the interpolation matrix diagonal.

Examples
--------
>>> interp = RBFInterpolator(kernel="gaussian", eps=2.0)
>>> interp.fit(source_pts, source_vals)
>>> u_query = interp(query_pts)      # (Q,)
>>> grad_u  = interp.gradient(query_pts)   # (Q, d)

methods.name: fit
methods.doc: Fit the interpolant to scattered data.

methods.name: gradient
methods.doc: Gradient of the interpolant at query_pts.

classes.name: ImplicitSurfaceRBF
classes.sig: (kernel: str = 'gaussian', eps: float = 2.0, offset: float = 0.01, reg: float = 1e-08) -> None
classes.doc:
Reconstruct a continuous SDF approximation from a point cloud with normals.

Fits an RBF interpolant to three constraint sets:

- On-surface samples (N pts):  SDF = 0
- Interior samples  (N pts):   pt - normal * offset  →  SDF = -offset
- Exterior samples  (N pts):   pt + normal * offset  →  SDF = +offset

The resulting function approximates the signed distance function (negative
inside, positive outside) of the surface. This enables using a raw point
cloud as a PINN geometry domain without building an explicit mesh.

The reconstructed SDF can be passed directly to functions expecting a
``SDF2D = Callable[[ndarray], ndarray]`` signature (e.g. ``mesh_sdf_2d``,
``sdf2d_to_pointcloud``, ``SDFDomain2D``).

Parameters
----------
kernel : RBF kernel for the interpolant
eps : shape parameter
offset : offset magnitude for off-surface constraints (world units).
    Tip: use ~1% of the characteristic domain size.
reg : Tikhonov regularisation for the linear system

Examples
--------
>>> surf = ImplicitSurfaceRBF(eps=3.0, offset=0.02)
>>> surf.fit(boundary_pts, normals)
>>> u_col = surf.sample_interior(5000, bounds_min, bounds_max)
>>> u_bc  = surf.sample_boundary(2000)
>>> d_vals = surf.sdf(query_pts)   # (Q,) SDF values

methods.doc: Fit the implicit surface from a point cloud with outward normals.

methods.name: sdf
methods.doc: Evaluate the reconstructed SDF at query_pts.

methods.name: is_inside
methods.doc: Boolean mask — True where SDF < 0 (inside the surface).

methods.doc: Sample n interior points via rejection using the reconstructed SDF.

methods.doc: Return n samples near the surface from the fitted point cloud.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.occ_features
children.doc:
Direct, parametric OpenCASCADE (OCC) solid-modeling feature operations.

This module exposes real fillet/chamfer/shell operations on an arbitrary
B-Rep solid (e.g. one imported from STEP, or produced by any of the
``cadquery_gen`` parametric builders) -- not just operations baked into a
builder function at construction time.

Kernel binding actually used in this repo
------------------------------------------
The two CAD-kernel bindings that ship as real, importable dependencies here
are ``cadquery`` (2.8.0) and its own compiled OCC wrapper, ``OCP``
(cadquery vendors/depends on OCP, which in turn wraps a real OpenCASCADE
build -- there is no separate "fake" CAD kernel involved). Neither
``pythonocc-core`` (the ``OCC`` package) nor FreeCAD's own bindings
(``FreeCAD`` / ``Part``) are installed in this environment -- both were
checked directly (``import OCC`` / ``import FreeCAD`` / ``import Part``)
and both raise ``ModuleNotFoundError``. FreeCAD's Python bindings are not
pip-installable in the usual sense (they ship inside a full FreeCAD
application/AppImage/conda build), so we do not attempt to fake that here.

Given that, this module is built directly on **cadquery's ``Workplane``
API**, which is itself a thin, well-documented layer over real OCP/OCC
B-Rep algorithms (not a re-implementation):

  * ``fillet_edges``  -> ``cadquery.Workplane.fillet`` -> internally builds
    ``cadquery.occ_impl.shapes.Solid.fillet`` -> real OCP class
    ``OCP.BRepFilletAPI.BRepFilletAPI_MakeFillet`` (constant-radius edge
    fillet). Verified by reading the installed cadquery 2.8.0 source
    (``cadquery/occ_impl/shapes.py``) in this environment.
  * ``chamfer_edges`` -> ``cadquery.Workplane.chamfer`` -> internally
    ``cadquery.occ_impl.shapes.Solid.chamfer`` -> real OCP class
    ``OCP.BRepFilletAPI.BRepFilletAPI_MakeChamfer``.
  * ``shell_solid`` -> ``cadquery.Workplane.shell`` -> internally
    ``cadquery.occ_impl.shapes.Mixin3D.hollow`` -> real OCP class
    ``OCP.BRepOffsetAPI.BRepOffsetAPI_MakeThickSolid`` (variable-offset
    thick-solid / hollowing operation).

We deliberately do *not* reach past cadquery's public Workplane API down to
raw ``OCP`` calls ourselves: cadquery's own wrappers already do exactly
that (see above), already handle the required edge/face -> solid parent
chain bookkeeping that the raw OCP fillet/chamfer/thicksolid builders need,
and are what the rest of this repo's CAD code (``cadquery_gen.py``)
already builds on. Duplicating that plumbing against raw ``OCP`` symbols
would be strictly less honest, not more -- it would just be a
reimplementation of the same calls cited above with more surface area for
bugs.

Object type in / object type out
---------------------------------
Every function here accepts and returns a ``cadquery.Workplane`` -- the
same "real object type" that ``cadquery_gen.py`` builds, converts, and
exports elsewhere in this repo (all of its example builders, e.g.
``cold_plate_channel`` / ``finned_plate``, return ``cq.Workplane``
objects; ``build_mesh_from_cadquery_object`` / ``export_cadquery`` accept
them directly). For convenience a raw ``cadquery.Solid`` / ``cadquery.Shape``
is also accepted and normalized into a ``Workplane`` on the way in.

functions.name: fillet_edges
functions.sig: (solid: Any, radius: float, edge_selector: EdgeSelector = None)
functions.doc:
Apply a real, parametric constant-radius fillet to a solid's edges.

Real OCC API used: ``cadquery.Workplane.fillet`` -> internally
``cadquery.occ_impl.shapes.Solid.fillet`` -> real OCP class
``OCP.BRepFilletAPI.BRepFilletAPI_MakeFillet`` (one ``.Add(radius, edge)``
call per selected edge, then ``.Shape()``).

Parameters
----------
solid:
    A ``cadquery.Workplane`` (or raw ``Solid``/``Shape``) wrapping a
    single solid -- e.g. the result of ``cadquery.importers.importStep``
    or any ``cadquery_gen`` builder output.
radius:
    Fillet radius, must be > 0.
edge_selector:
    Optional cadquery edge selector (a selector string such as
    ``"|Z"``/``">Z"`` or a ``cadquery.selectors.Selector`` instance).
    ``None`` (default) selects *all* edges of the solid, matching
    ``Workplane.edges()`` with no arguments.

Returns
-------
cadquery.Workplane
    A new Workplane with the filleted solid selected on the stack.

functions.name: chamfer_edges
functions.sig: (solid: Any, distance: float, edge_selector: EdgeSelector = None)
functions.doc:
Apply a real, parametric chamfer to a solid's edges.

Real OCC API used: ``cadquery.Workplane.chamfer`` -> internally
``cadquery.occ_impl.shapes.Solid.chamfer`` -> real OCP class
``OCP.BRepFilletAPI.BRepFilletAPI_MakeChamfer`` (edge/face pairs are
resolved via an OCP ``TopTools_IndexedDataMapOfShapeListOfShape``
edge->face map, then one ``.Add(d1, d2, edge, face)`` call per edge).

Parameters
----------
solid:
    A ``cadquery.Workplane`` (or raw ``Solid``/``Shape``) wrapping a
    single solid.
distance:
    Chamfer length, must be > 0.
edge_selector:
    Optional cadquery edge selector. ``None`` (default) selects all
    edges of the solid.

Returns
-------
cadquery.Workplane
    A new Workplane with the chamfered solid selected on the stack.

functions.name: shell_solid
functions.sig: (solid: Any, thickness: float, faces_to_remove: FaceSelector = None)
functions.doc:
Hollow out a solid into a shell of the given wall thickness.

Real OCC API used: ``cadquery.Workplane.shell`` -> internally
``cadquery.occ_impl.shapes.Mixin3D.hollow`` -> real OCP class
``OCP.BRepOffsetAPI.BRepOffsetAPI_MakeThickSolid``
(``MakeThickSolidByJoin`` with the removed-faces list, thickness and
join type).

Parameters
----------
solid:
    A ``cadquery.Workplane`` (or raw ``Solid``/``Shape``) wrapping a
    single solid.
thickness:
    Wall thickness. Positive shells outward, negative shells inward
    (per ``BRepOffsetAPI_MakeThickSolid`` semantics); must be nonzero.
faces_to_remove:
    Optional cadquery face selector (e.g. ``">Z"`` to open up the top
    face, matching ``Workplane.faces(...)``) picking which face(s) to
    remove/open. ``None`` (default) removes *no* faces, which produces
    a fully-enclosed hollow solid with an internal cavity (the
    ``hollow()`` "no faces provided" branch that constructs a
    watertight offset shell via ``BRepBuilderAPI_MakeSolid``).

Returns
-------
cadquery.Workplane
    A new Workplane with the shelled solid selected on the stack.

Geometry retrieval: find the parts most similar to a query part.

Use: before training a surrogate for a new part, look for a similar part that already has one
(transfer / fine-tune instead of starting from scratch), or deduplicate a CAD library.

Two sources of vectors, one index:

- :func:`shape_descriptor` -- no ML, works offline on any mesh: the D2 shape distribution
  (histogram of distances between random surface point pairs, normalised by their mean; Osada,
  Funkhouser, Chazelle & Dobkin, "Shape distributions", ACM Trans. Graph. 21(4) (2002) 807-832),
  concatenated with sorted principal extents. Invariant to rotation, translation and scale.
- precomputed embeddings, e.g. the ~1M ABC parts rendered, captioned by a VLM and text-embedded
  by finalrev ("Embedding one million 3D models", 2026; HF ``daveferbear/3d-model-images-embeddings``,
  no license declared, ABC/Onshape origin -> research only, see ``pinneapple_catalog``):
  :func:`load_caption_index` builds an index over its parquet shards, with keyword search on the
  captions and neighbour search between parts. Its embedding model is not published, so new text
  queries cannot be embedded into that space; keyword search on captions is used instead.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.runner_ramp
children.doc:
Rampa do canal de corrida (família Capture02): geometria paramétrica e sólido fechado.

Um só lugar para os parâmetros da rampa. Nasceu de uma divergência real: dois estudos simularam "a mesma rampa" e
chegaram a escoamentos diferentes porque cada equipe materializou os parâmetros à sua maneira — a nossa subia do
piso a partir de 3,5 m, 100/250/400 mm acima dele; o sólido do CAD desce da crista, que fica acima do nível do banho,
começa em 4,228 m e tem pé residual de 472 a 772 mm. Fixar a definição aqui (coordenadas globais, sem altura relativa
ao piso) é a correção de fundo.

Convenções, todas em metros e no referencial do CFD do canal (`canal.stp`):

- ``s`` é a distância ao plano de entrada, ``s = y - y_origem`` com ``y_origem = -7.429``; ``s = 0`` é o plano de
  entrada, que é o "centroide da entrada" da outra equipe a 1 mm (o centroide fica em ``y = -7.427945``).
- ``z_crista`` e ``z_pe`` são cotas **globais** do CFD, não alturas acima do piso.
- a rampa é centrada no eixo lateral do canal, ``x_eixo = -2.111`` (paredes em ``x = -2.544`` e ``-1.678``).

Forma (a do CAD, descrita pela outra equipe): face vertical a montante na crista; face reta descendente com a
inclinação publicada; pé curvo, ocupando 35 % do trecho inclinado, com tangência contínua no patamar; patamar
horizontal; face vertical a jusante. O trecho inclinado é resolvido para cair exatamente ``z_crista - z_pe``, o que
reproduz o patamar de 0,25 m das cinco variantes.

O piso é o do CAD, linear em ``s`` (3,5 m: -2,848; 5 m: -2,883), conferido contra o STEP até 9 m dentro de 2 mm.

Uso::

    from pinneapple_design.geometry.runner_ramp import CASOS, perfil, solido, validar
    perfil(CASOS["V02"], 5.0)                 # cota do topo da rampa em s = 5,0 m
    verts, faces = solido(CASOS["V02"])       # sólido fechado, pronto para STL/STL binário
    validar()                                 # comparação com as cotas publicadas do CAD

``validar()`` é o teste de referência desta geometria: as alturas da crista e do pé acima do fundo, medidas no
sólido, têm de bater com as do CAD publicado dentro de 3 mm.

functions.name: sample_barycentric_uv
functions.sig: (n: int, rng: Optional[np.random.Generator] = None) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]

Sample barycentric weights (w0, w1, w2) uniformly over a triangle.

  u, v ~ U(0,1)

  w0 = 1 - su
  w1 = su * (1 - v)
  w2 = su * v

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.trough
children.doc:
Longitudinal section of a melt runner (trough) as a 2-D OpenFOAM mesh: a sloped floor, a weir (skimmer) at the
downstream end, a jet entering through the top, and open air above.

    from pinneapple_design.geometry.trough import TroughSection
    sec = TroughSection(length=8.0, slope_deg=2.0)         # + slope: the floor descends toward the weir
    sec.write_mesh("cases/trough/mesh")                     # blockMesh; patches floor, upstream, weir,
                                                            # outlet, inlet, atmosphere, frontAndBack (empty)

The mesh is in the trough's own frame (x along the floor, z normal to it) and stays rectangular: the slope enters
through gravity, tilted by ``slope_deg`` (``gravity()``), with the bath surface normal to it (``level()``) and the
jet velocity rotated into the same frame (``to_mesh``). The floor pivots about the weir end, so a slope keeps the
weir crest and the bath level and changes the depth under the jet: +2° (floor descending toward the weir) gives a
shallow pool at impact, -2° a deep one. A sloped mesh with vertical gravity was unstable in the shallow corner in
interFoam (v1912); the tilted-gravity frame is the standard equivalent. Six blocks: three columns (upstream, jet,
downstream) times two rows (below and above the weir crest).

methods.doc: Floor height above the weir-end floor in the world frame (for plots).

methods.name: depth_at
methods.doc: Initial bath depth, measured vertically (the bath fills to the weir crest).

methods.name: gravity
methods.doc: Gravity in the mesh frame.

methods.name: to_mesh
methods.doc: A world-frame vector (x downstream, z up) in the mesh frame.

methods.name: level
methods.doc: The bath surface through the weir crest, as a height along -gravity (FreeSurfaceFlow ``level``).

methods.sig: (case: str, bashrc: str | None = None) -> str
methods.doc: Write system/blockMeshDict (with a minimal controlDict) and run blockMesh; returns ``case``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicle_cad
children.doc:
Parametric vehicle CAD: closed-mesh primitives for rover-class vehicles, parts with materials and masses, mass
properties (centre of mass and inertia from the meshes) and assembly into bodies for multibody simulation.

    from pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicle_cad import VehicleCAD, beveled_box, rover_wheel, solar_panel
    cad = VehicleCAD("my rover")
    cad.add("chassis", "body", beveled_box((1.2, 0.9, 0.5), (0, 0, 0.8), 0.03), "white_paint", mass=200.0)
    cad.add("wheel_FL", "wheel_FL", *rover_wheel(0.25, 0.2, grousers=24, grouser_height=0.025))  # several parts
    props = cad.mass_properties()          # per body: mass, com, inertia about the com (body frame = world here)
    cad.scene().save("rover.glb")          # glTF with PBR materials, .stl, .usda

A *part* is one closed triangle mesh with a material and a mass (uniform density inside the mesh); a *body* is a
group of parts that move together (chassis, a suspension arm, a wheel). Parts that are thin plates are still closed
boxes so volume, centroid and inertia are well defined (divergence theorem, Eberly's polyhedral mass properties).

Coordinates: metres, z up, x forward, y left. Every function returns ``(vertices (V, 3), faces (F, 3))`` or, for the
assemblies (wheel, panel, camera head ...), a list of ``(suffix, (V, F), material, mass_share)``.

Closed solid skinned through ``rings`` (m, n, 3): m closed polylines of n points each, in corresponding order.

Consecutive rings are joined by quads; both ends are capped, either with a fan from the ring centroid
(``cap="fan"``, right for convex or star-shaped rings) or with a strip joining point ``j`` to point ``n-1-j``

Rotary actuator in assembly coordinates: a cylindrical housing from ``p0`` to ``p1`` (output end at ``p0``),
flange rings at both ends and a motor / gearbox cap beyond ``p1`` (BLDC motor plus strain-wave gear class
joints: suspension, steering, mast pan).

functions.sig: (width: float = 0.36, depth: float = 0.15, height: float = 0.12, baseline: float = 0.24, lens_radius: float = 0.02, lights: int = 6, aft_camera: bool = True, pan_height: float = 0.06)
functions.doc:
Mast head on a pan-tilt unit, in its own frame (pan axis = z through the origin, looking +x): pan drum, a
U-yoke carrying the tilt axle, a camera box with a stereo pair of lenses ``baseline`` apart, a row of
``lights`` LEDs under them and an optional aft-looking camera. The top of the head is at
``pan_height + 0.02 + height``.

Rotary-percussive planetary drill with a deployment rail, in its own frame: drill axis = z through the origin,
footpad bottom at z = 0, the rail frame (and the mount face) on the -x side. Parts: a ladder guide rail of
``rail_height`` with a backing deployment stage, the drill head (rotary-percussive housing and motor) riding on
a carriage, the auger stem with its helical flight and the bit, a cuttings brush station and chute near the
bottom, and the footpad ring. ``carriage`` in [0, 1] places the head along its feed stroke (1 = stowed at the
top, 0 = fully fed: the feed stroke is ``rail_height - head height - 0.10``; the travel of the deployment
stage, which lowers the rail and footpad to the ground, is not modelled).

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d
children.doc:
Parametric 3-D vehicles for CFD and photoreal rendering: a road car and a launch vehicle.

Both return ``Part`` lists (``pinneapple_design.aero.airframe.Part``: name, vertices, faces, material, group, aero),
in metres, x along the vehicle from the nose (the flow direction), z up, symmetric about y = 0. The parts with
``aero=True`` are closed surfaces that form the CFD geometry; the others (rims, the rocket's engine bells and plume)
are only drawn. Materials are names from ``VEHICLE_MATERIALS`` (registered with the studio on import).

    from pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d import RoadCar, LaunchVehicle
    car = RoadCar(style="fastback", slant_deg=22)
    parts = car.parts()                      # body (paint / glass / lights / trim faces), four wheels
    bodies = car.cfd_bodies()                # {"body": (V, F), "wheels": (V, F)} for ExternalFlow (ground at z = 0)
    rocket = LaunchVehicle()
    rocket.barrowman()                       # normal-force slope and centre of pressure, Barrowman's equations

classes.doc:
A four-door coupé / sedan: ``style`` "fastback" (roof runs into a slanted rear window down to the tail) or
"notchback" (rear window, then a trunk deck). Dimensions in metres.

methods.doc: Projected frontal area (body and wheels), from a fine raster of the y-z projection.

methods.doc: The parts stood on their tail (nose up, z), for launch renders.

methods.name: barrowman
methods.doc:
Normal-force slope CN_alpha (per rad, on the body cross-section) and centre of pressure from the nose,
by Barrowman's equations (subsonic, small angles): ogive nose CN_a = 2 at 0.466 of its length; the fairing
shoulder (boat-tail to the stage diameter) as a conical transition; four fins with body interference.

classes.name: FormulaCar
classes.doc:
A parametric open-wheel racing car in the spirit of current Formula 1 (not any team's car): monocoque with
sidepods and engine cover, floor with a diffuser, multi-element front and rear wings with endplates (DRS flap
open or closed), driver helmet, halo and four exposed wheels. Metres, x from the front-wing leading edge, z up
from the road, symmetric about y = 0.

``cfd_bodies()`` returns the closed surfaces separately (body, floor, front_wing, rear_wing, helmet, wheels) so the
CFD reports drag and downforce per component; the halo and the rims are drawn only.

methods.doc:
Projected frontal area (m^2) of the CFD shape: every aero triangle rasterised on the y-z plane at
``px`` metres per pixel.

Closed NACA 4-digit profile (x, z) on a unit chord, trailing edge -> upper surface -> leading edge -> lower
surface, with a finite trailing edge (0.3 % thick) so the solid stays closed.

children.doc:
pinneapple_geom

Geometry + mesh utilities for Pinneapple.

MVP-1 focus (trimesh + meshio):
- Load geometry files (STL/OBJ/PLY/GLTF/...)
- Load mesh files (VTK/VTU/MSH/...)
- Generate simple parametric primitives -> meshes
- Apply fast transforms (scale/translate/rotate)
- Provide surface sampling hooks for PINN collocation/BC points

Design principles:
- Keep `pinneapple_geom` independent from `pinneapple_pdb` (ETL) and `pinneapple_pinn` (loss/models)
- Expose a small stable API surface from `__init__`

pinneapple_design.geometry_library.core
children.doc:
Registry, parameter specs and the :class:`Geometry` object returned by :func:`build`.

A library entry is a :class:`GeometrySpec`: a builder ``fn(p, res) -> list[Body]`` (``p`` the physical parameters
with defaults filled in, ``res`` a resolution multiplier set by the level of detail), the documented parameters with
ranges, the documented overall dimensions, the reference frame, the sources of the real-world numbers and the
intended physics uses. Entries register themselves on import (``entries/``).

classes.doc: One physical parameter: default, unit, admissible range (inclusive), what it controls.

classes.name: Source
classes.doc:
Where a real-world number comes from. ``estimate=True`` flags a value chosen by eye or by engineering
judgement (no published figure).

classes.name: Body
classes.doc:
One closed surface (watertight, outward normals) or, with ``closed=False``, an open sheet that is drawn only.

``materials`` is one material name, or one name per face (a livery, windows, lights on one closed skin).
``aero=True`` bodies form the physics shape (CFD / FEA); the others are details drawn only.

methods.doc: Sum of the enclosed volumes of the closed bodies (overlaps counted twice; see :meth:`solid`).

methods.doc:
Boolean union of the closed bodies: one watertight, self-intersection-free surface for meshing
(needs ``manifold3d``).

pinneapple_design.geometry_library.entries.aircraft_new
children.doc:
Three rotor-driven aircraft from published figures: an ATR 72-600-class regional twin turboprop, an H145-class
light twin helicopter and an F450-frame-class quadcopter drone. Lifting surfaces and rotor / propeller blades are
lofted through NACA sections with twist (constant geometric pitch for the propellers, linear twist for the main

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry_library.exporters
children.doc:
File writers: binary STL, OBJ (+ MTL), glTF binary, OpenUSD (ASCII) and STEP (faceted B-rep).

Every writer is deterministic (same geometry -> same bytes), which lets the manifest pin each file with SHA-256.
STEP is written as an AP214 ``FACETED_BREP`` per closed body (planar triangular faces bounded by poly-loops), which
OpenCASCADE / FreeCAD / CATIA / NX import as solids; :func:`step_check` reads it back through OpenCASCADE when
``cadquery`` is installed.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry_library.kit
children.doc:
Closed-surface building blocks for the library entries (z up, metres, outward normals).

Every function returns ``(V, F)``; every surface is closed (watertight) unless the name says otherwise:
lofts through rings with capped or pole ends, solids of revolution, NACA sections and lofted wings / blades,
rounded boxes, cylinders, frusta, ellipsoids, swept tubes, extruded polygons (ear-clipped caps), rotations.

functions.name: rot
functions.sig: (axis, angle_deg: float) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: tf
functions.sig: (mesh: Mesh, R = None, t = (0, 0, 0), about = (0, 0, 0), scale = 1.0) -> Mesh

functions.name: mirror
functions.sig: (mesh: Mesh, axis: int = 1) -> Mesh

functions.name: with_mirror
functions.sig: (mesh: Mesh, axis: int = 1) -> list[Mesh]

functions.name: merge
functions.sig: (meshes: Iterable[Mesh]) -> Mesh

functions.name: ear_clip_fast
functions.sig: (P2: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Ear clipping of a simple polygon (counter-clockwise), vectorised point-in-triangle tests; (n - 2, 3).

functions.name: loft
functions.sig: (rings, start: str = 'cap', end: str = 'cap') -> Mesh
functions.doc:
Closed surface through closed rings ``(n_rings, n, 3)``. ``start`` / ``end``: "cap" (flat end: a fan to the
centroid, or an ear-clipped triangulation for a concave ring) or "pole" (the end ring is joined to its centroid:
a pointed / rounded tip, the centroid can be moved afterwards).

functions.name: revolve
functions.sig: (x, r, n: int = 48, axis: str = 'x', center = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), phase: float = 0.0) -> Mesh
functions.doc:
Solid of revolution of the meridian ``r(x)`` about an axis through ``center``. End stations with r = 0
close as poles, others are capped.

functions.name: superellipse
functions.sig: (hw: float, hh: float, n: int, e: float = 2.0, zc: float = 0.0, yc: float = 0.0, top_e: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Ring of ``n`` (y, z) points: |y/hw|^e + |z/hh|^e = 1 (``top_e``: another exponent for the upper half).

functions.name: body_of_sections
functions.sig: (xs, hw, zb, zt, n: int = 48, e = 2.4, e_top = None) -> Mesh
functions.doc: Fuselage-like body: at station x, a super-ellipse of half-width hw(x) between z = zb(x) and z = zt(x).

functions.name: naca4
functions.sig: (m: float = 0.0, p: float = 0.4, t: float = 0.12, n: int = 40, closed_te: bool = True) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
NACA 4-digit outline, ``(2n - 2, 2)`` points, counter-clockwise from the trailing edge over the upper surface
(x in [0, 1] from the leading edge, y up). ``closed_te`` uses the -0.1036 coefficient (sharp trailing edge).

functions.name: thick_te
functions.sig: (sec: np.ndarray, te: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Open the trailing edge to a finite thickness ``te`` (fraction of chord), linearly from the leading edge.

functions.name: section_ring
functions.sig: (sec2d: np.ndarray, chord: float, twist_deg: float, le, frame = None, pivot: float = 0.25) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Place a unit-chord section in 3D: chord along ``frame[0]``, thickness along ``frame[1]``, twisted by
``twist_deg`` about ``pivot`` x chord (nose-up positive), leading edge at ``le``.

functions.name: wing
functions.sig: (stations: Sequence[dict], n: int = 36, frame = None, tip: str = 'cap') -> Mesh
functions.doc:
Loft through wing / blade stations. Each station: ``le`` (3,), ``chord``, ``twist`` (deg), ``t`` (t/c),
``m`` / ``p`` (camber), optional ``section`` (a 2D outline overriding the NACA one). Closed at both ends.

functions.name: blend_sections
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, w: float) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: round_section
functions.sig: (n: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: A unit circle as a 'section' (x in [0, 1]) with the same point count as :func:`naca4` (``2n - 2``).

functions.name: box

functions.doc:
Box with every edge and corner rounded by ``radius`` (absolute): the Minkowski sum of a smaller box and a

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry_library.meshops
children.doc:
Mesh operations for the library: welding, orientation, watertightness, volume, self-intersection, union.

NumPy / SciPy only, except :func:`union` (``manifold3d``). Meshes are ``(V (n, 3) float, F (m, 3) int)``.

functions.name: concat
functions.sig: (meshes: Sequence[Mesh]) -> Mesh

functions.name: compact
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> Mesh
functions.doc: Drop unreferenced vertices.

functions.name: weld
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, tol: float = 1e-09) -> Mesh
functions.doc: Merge coincident vertices (quantised to ``tol`` relative to the size), drop collapsed faces.

functions.name: area
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> float

functions.name: volume
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc: Signed enclosed volume (positive for outward normals).

functions.name: face_normals
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, unit: bool = True) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: edge_stats
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, int]
functions.doc:
Counts after welding: boundary edges (used once), non-manifold edges (> 2), edges whose two faces disagree
on the winding.

functions.name: components
functions.sig: (F: np.ndarray, n_vertices: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Connected-component label of every face (faces sharing a vertex).

functions.name: orient_outward
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> Mesh
functions.doc: Flip each closed component whose signed volume is negative (the winding inside a component is kept).

functions.name: quality
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, closed: bool = True) -> dict[str, float]

functions.name: self_intersections
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, max_pairs: int = 20000000, return_pairs: bool = False)
functions.doc:
Number of intersecting pairs of non-adjacent triangles. Candidate pairs come from k-d trees on the triangle
centres, bucketed by circumradius (powers of two), so a few large cap triangles do not blow up the search.

functions.name: union
functions.sig: (meshes: Sequence[Mesh]) -> Mesh
functions.doc: Boolean union of closed meshes with ``manifold3d`` (``pip install manifold3d``).

functions.name: crease_normals
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, angle_deg: float = 38.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Per-corner normals ``(m, 3, 3)``: the smooth vertex normal where it is within ``angle_deg`` of the face
normal, the face normal across creases (sharp box edges stay sharp).

functions.name: solidify
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, thickness: float)
functions.doc:
Close an open sheet into a thin shell: the sheet, a copy offset by ``-thickness`` along the vertex normals
with reversed winding, and side walls along the boundary edges. Returns ``(V, F, kept)`` where ``kept`` marks
the original faces that survived welding.

functions.name: fix_winding
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray) -> Mesh
functions.doc:
Make the winding consistent across every edge-manifold component (breadth-first propagation over shared
edges), then orient each component outward.

functions.name: refan_concave_caps
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, materials = None, min_valence: int = 5)
functions.doc:
Re-triangulate flat cap fans that fold over themselves: a vertex whose incident faces are coplanar and whose
link loop is not star-shaped around it (a fan to the centroid of a cambered airfoil cap) is removed and its loop
ear-clipped. Returns ``(V, F, materials)`` (unreferenced centre vertices are left in ``V``).

children.summary: Mesh operations for the library: welding, orientation, watertightness, volume, self-intersection, union.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry_library.render
children.doc:
Software renderer for thumbnails, the contact sheet and the turntable GIF (NumPy + Pillow, no GPU, no Blender).

Deferred rasteriser: every triangle is scan-converted into a z-buffer that keeps the triangle id and barycentric
coordinates per pixel, then all pixels are shaded at once (perspective-correct normals with sharp creases,
physically-flavoured PBR: Lambert + Blinn-Phong with roughness, metallic reflections of a studio sky, Fresnel rim,
emissive), a shadow map from the key light, a soft contact shadow on a ground disc, screen-space ambient occlusion
and 2x supersampling. Deterministic: the same geometry renders the same image.

For photoreal renders use Blender through ``pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.render(geom.scene(), ...)``.

functions.name: rasterize
functions.sig: (sx, sy, depth, F, W, H, persp = True, max_frag = 3000000)
functions.doc:
Scan-convert triangles. ``sx, sy``: pixel coordinates of the vertices, ``depth``: positive distance.
Returns (zbuf, tri id (-1 = empty), b0, b1) of shape (H, W).

functions.name: render_geometry
functions.sig: (geom, path: str | None = None, size: tuple[int, int] = (960, 640), azimuth: float | None = None, elevation: float | None = None, ssaa: int = 2, background: str = 'studio', fov_deg: float = 28.0, ground: bool | None = None, margin: float = 0.9, label: str | None = None, frame: tuple[Sequence[float], Sequence[float]] | None = None)
functions.doc:
Render ``geom`` (a library :class:`Geometry`) and return a PIL image (also saved to ``path`` if given).

``azimuth`` / ``elevation`` (degrees) default to the entry's camera; azimuth 0 looks from +x (behind for
vehicles, whose x points aft), measured toward +y. ``frame``: (lo, hi) corners of a box to frame instead of
the geometry's own bounds, so the frames of an animation share one camera.

functions.name: contact_sheet
functions.sig: (geoms: Sequence, path: str, cols: int = 4, tile: tuple[int, int] = (480, 330), title: str = '') -> str
functions.doc: Grid of thumbnails with names (PNG).

functions.name: turntable
functions.sig: (geoms: Sequence, path: str, frames: int = 24, cols: int = 4, tile: tuple[int, int] = (240, 165), duration_ms: int = 90) -> str
functions.doc: Animated GIF: every geometry spinning once, in a grid.

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry_library.store
children.doc:
Pre-generated files: the manifest (SHA-256 of every file), the local copies, the Hugging Face Hub, the cache.

Light files (STL + glTF) are committed under ``data/geometries/<name>/`` and the thumbnails under
``docs/assets/geometry_library/``; every format of both levels
of detail is published to the Hub dataset ``PINNeAPPle-Labs/geometry-library`` by the ``geometry-library``
workflow. :func:`load` looks, in order, in the repository copy, the cache (``~/.cache/pinneapple/geometries`` or
``$PINNEAPPLE_GEOMETRY_CACHE``) and the Hub, checks the SHA-256 against the manifest, and, if the file cannot be
had (offline, not uploaded yet, or a hash mismatch), builds it from the code with the default parameters, which
reproduce the stored files.

Environment: ``PINNEAPPLE_GEOMETRY_HUB`` (another Hub repo id), ``PINNEAPPLE_GEOMETRY_CACHE``,
``PINNEAPPLE_OFFLINE=1`` or ``HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`` (never touch the network).

children.name: pinneapple_design.geometry_library.web
children.doc:
The geometry library for the browser: an index of every entry and small thumbnails.

    python -m pinneapple_design.geometry_library.web data/web/geometries

``index.json`` lists, per geometry, what a gallery card needs: title, category, description, dimensions, triangle
count, the light glTF file (repo path and Hub URL), the sources of the dimensions (estimates flagged), the physics
it is built for, its parameters, a link to the builder's source and the code that regenerates it.
``thumbs/<name>.jpg`` are 360x240 JPEGs of the committed renders (``docs/assets/geometry_library``).

functions.doc: The gallery index (see the module docstring).

functions.doc: Write ``index.json`` and ``thumbs/<name>.jpg`` into ``directory``; returns the index.

children.doc:
Geometry library: realistic parametric 3-D geometries for Physics-AI, with the code that regenerates them and
ready-made files.

    import pinneapple as pp
    pp.geometries.list()                                   # every entry
    pp.geometries.info("wind_turbine_nrel5mw")             # dimensions, parameters with ranges, sources, uses
    g = pp.geometries.build("wind_turbine_nrel5mw", pitch_deg=5.0)   # -> Geometry (closed bodies, materials)
    g.export("turbine.stl"); g.export("turbine.glb"); g.export("turbine.step")
    g.render("turbine.png")                                # thumbnail (software renderer)
    pp.geometries.load("airliner_a320", format="glb")      # path to the pre-generated file (repo, cache or Hub)

Every entry is in metres in a documented frame, made of closed, outward-oriented bodies, at two levels of detail
(``lod="light"``: committed, ~20k triangles; ``"fine"``: on the Hugging Face Hub). ``build`` with the default
parameters reproduces the stored files (tested). ``Geometry.solid()`` fuses the bodies into one watertight surface
for meshing (``manifold3d``). See ``docs/guides/geometry_library.md``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.intent.parse
children.doc:
Intent -> RequirementSpec: pick a template, read the numbers with their units, fill the template's slots.

The deterministic parser needs no network: it finds every ``number unit`` pair (``2 kN``, ``40W``, ``85 °C``,
``30 cm``), checks the unit with :mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`, and gives each to the slot of the same
dimension whose keywords are closest in the sentence. Phrases map to values through the slots' cues ("still air" ->
0 m/s). Nothing is guessed: a value it cannot place is reported as unused, a critical slot it cannot fill becomes a
question.

An LLM can be plugged in behind :class:`IntentLLM` (anything with ``extract(text, schema) -> dict``). Its answer is
used only where it can be checked: the template must exist, every value must come with a quote that occurs in the
text and contains the number, and the unit must have the slot's dimension. The deterministic reading wins on
conflicts.

children.name: pinneapple_design.intent.physics.loop_track
children.doc:
Loop-the-loop track for a small car: the track curve, a 1-D model of the car along it, the closed form, and the
Newton rigid-body scene of the same track.

The track lies in the x-z plane (z up), the car runs in +x and turns counter-clockwise through the loop. It is made
of five pieces: a launch run, an entry clothoid (curvature rising linearly from 0 to 1/R), a circular arc of radius R,
an exit clothoid (1/R back to 0) and a run-out. With clothoid length 0 the loop is a circle. In 3-D the loop is a
helix: the exit is shifted sideways by ``pitch`` (a smoothstep, no sideways kink) so that it clears the entry, the way
real toy tracks are built.

Three models of the same car on the same track, from cheap to expensive:

``closed_form``
    Energy balance with the loss terms evaluated at a mean speed, the top-of-loop condition
    ``v_top^2 >= g R`` (normal force >= 0) and the peak load at the end of the entry clothoid.
``along_track``
    The car as a point on its centre-of-mass path (the track offset by the CoM height ``h``), with the normal force
    ``N = m (v^2 kappa + g cos theta)``, rolling resistance ``C_rr N``, aerodynamic drag ``0.5 rho C_d A v^2`` and the
    rotating wheels as an added inertia. ``d(v^2)/ds`` is integrated with fourth-order Runge-Kutta, vectorised over
    many designs.
``newton_check``
    The car as a rigid sphere of the wheel radius in contact with the 3-D track mesh (strip and side rails, the
    helical exit), integrated by NVIDIA Newton (XPBD). It checks the track geometry, the contact and the loop
    dynamics in 3-D; Newton has no air, and its contact dissipates a few per cent of the energy on the curved mesh,
    so the run is judged against the worst-case envelope of the 1-D model rather than for equality.

methods.name: turn_clothoid
methods.doc: Heading change of one clothoid [rad] (curvature 0 -> 1/R over its length).

methods.name: curvature
methods.doc: Signed curvature [1/m] at arc length ``s`` of the running surface.

methods.name: loop_span
methods.doc: Arc-length interval of the loop proper (entry clothoid start to exit clothoid end).

methods.name: sample
methods.doc:
The running surface at ``n`` points: ``s, x, y, z, theta`` (heading from +x, rad), ``kappa``,
``nx, nz`` (unit normal pointing to the car's side). Integrated with the trapezoid rule on a fine grid.

methods.name: footprint
methods.doc: Length along x of the whole track [m].

classes.name: Run
classes.doc:
Result of the 1-D model for a batch of designs (arrays of shape ``(n_designs,)``) plus the profiles of the
first design.

functions.name: along_track
functions.sig: (radius, clothoid, v0, mass, *, crr = 0.02, cd = 0.6, area = 0.0006, com_height = 0.008, wheel_inertia = 0.0, rho = 1.204, g = G0, run_in = 0.3, run_out = 0.3, n = 1200) -> Run
functions.doc:
Integrate ``d(v^2)/ds`` along the centre-of-mass path for a batch of designs (all arguments broadcast).

``v0`` is the speed at the start of the launch run. The car fails when ``v^2`` reaches 0 (it stops and rolls
back) or when the normal force becomes negative (it leaves the track). Losses: ``C_rr max(N, 0)`` and
``0.5 rho C_d A v^2``; ``wheel_inertia`` adds ``sum I/r^2`` to the inertia (not to the weight).

functions.name: closed_form
functions.sig: (radius, clothoid, v0, mass, *, crr = 0.02, cd = 0.6, area = 0.0006, com_height = 0.008, wheel_inertia = 0.0, rho = 1.204, g = G0, run_in = 0.3) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Screening estimate (vectorised): energy to the top with the losses at the mean speed, the top condition and
the peak load.

The top of the loop is at height ``z_top`` of the centre-of-mass path (``2 R_c`` for a circular loop; the
clothoids raise it, computed from their Fresnel integrals). Losses from the start to the top: rolling
``C_rr m g`` on the run-in plus ``C_rr m v_m^2 theta_top`` in the turn (``int N ds ~ m v^2 dtheta`` with the
gravity terms cancelling over the half loop), and drag ``q v_m^2 s_top`` with ``v_m^2`` the mean of the launch
and top values (one fixed-point pass).

functions.name: track_meshes
functions.sig: (track: LoopTrack, thickness: float = 0.003, rail: float = 0.008, n: int = 600)
functions.doc:
Closed meshes of the running strip and the two side rails, in metres: ``{"strip": (V, F), "rail_l": ...}``.
The strip lies below the running surface (normal offset ``-thickness``..0).

functions.name: car_mesh
functions.sig: (length: float, width: float, height: float, wheel_r: float)
functions.doc: A simple car for drawings and files: rounded body plus four wheels, resting on z = 0, nose along +x.

functions.name: newton_scene
functions.sig: (track: LoopTrack, mass: float, v0: float, *, radius: float = 0.006, mu: float = 0.0, thickness: float = 0.003, rail: float = 0.008, n: int = 900)
functions.doc:
The track (one static triangle mesh: strip + rails) and the car as a sphere of the wheel radius resting on the
running surface, launched along +x, as a :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics.
RigidScene`.

functions.name: newton_check
functions.sig: (track: LoopTrack, mass: float, v0: float, *, dt: float = 2.5e-05, duration: float | None = None, iterations: int = 12, record_every: int | None = None, radius: float = 0.006, mu: float = 0.0) -> NewtonLoopResult
functions.doc:
Run the car through the loop in NVIDIA Newton (XPBD contact on the track mesh) and measure whether it stays
on the track and reaches the end, the speed at the top and the largest gap to the running surface in the loop.

children.doc:
Design from intent: a plain-language goal in, a buildable and verified design package out.

    import pinneapple as pp
    pkg = pp.design("I want a toy car that does a loop", out_dir="loop_design")
    print(pkg.summary())                      # design, verdict, probability, trust decision
    pp.design("a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air")   # -> NeedsInput: asks for the temperature limit

Stages (each a typed object): :func:`formulate` (text -> :class:`RequirementSpec`, values with units and provenance),
:func:`plan` (-> :class:`PhysicsPlan` from a registered :class:`ProblemTemplate`), :func:`optimise` (closed-form
screening, optimisation on the reduced model with the design-study core), :func:`robustness` (Monte Carlo),
:func:`verify` (full solver), :func:`assess` (trust report and verdict), :class:`DesignPackage` (files and report).
Requests outside every template return an :class:`OutOfScope` that says what would be needed.

children.name: pinneapple_design.qualitative
pinneapple_design.qualitative.descriptors
children.doc:
Geometric descriptors of closed triangulated bodies and assemblies of named parts.

Everything the qualitative models need comes from the surface mesh: per-face areas, normals and centroids, the
volume and second moments (exact polyhedral integrals over signed tetrahedra), extents, projected (frontal) area,
sharp edges, and section properties along an axis from a voxelization. An ``Assembly`` keeps the parts separate, so
a change to one part (scaled, moved, removed, replaced) can be traced to its physical effect.

classes.doc: Geometric descriptors of one body (SI units). ``direction`` is the flow / load reference direction.

classes.doc: Named parts of one geometry. Parts are treated as touching, not overlapping (areas add).

where it is attached at the low side) or a given point.

functions.sig: (geom: Any) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: ``(vertices, faces)`` from a tuple, a trimesh-like object (``.vertices``/``.faces``) or an ``Assembly``.

functions.doc:
Closed prism from a counter-clockwise 2-D polygon (n, 2) in the (x, z) plane, extruded along ``axis`` by
``depth`` (centred), so 2-D sections can be compared with the same models.

functions.doc: Per-face area, unit normal and centroid.

functions.sig: (geom: Any, direction = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) -> Descriptors
functions.doc:
Descriptors of a closed, outward-oriented triangulated body. The projected area is
``0.5 * sum |n . d| A`` (exact for convex bodies, an upper bound otherwise).

functions.name: section_profile
functions.sig: (geom: Any, axis: int = 0, n_slices: int = 40, n_grid: int | tuple[int, int] = 48)
functions.doc:
Section properties along ``axis`` from a voxelization by ray parity: slice positions ``x`` (centres), area
``A(x)``, centroid of each section in the two other coordinates, second moments ``I(x)`` about the section's
centroidal axes (``I_a``: about the first remaining axis, i.e. bending in the second; ``I_b`` the other way) and
the extreme fibre distances ``c_a``, ``c_b``. Also returns the voxel occupancy ``(n_slices, n_a, n_b)`` and the
cell sizes, e.g. for a voxel finite-element model. ``n_grid``: cells across the section (one number or a pair).

children.summary: Geometric descriptors of closed triangulated bodies and assemblies of named parts.

children.name: pinneapple_design.qualitative.models
children.doc:
Cheap physical models that turn a geometry into first estimates, the mechanisms behind them and a surface map.

They are meant for the qualitative step before any simulation: which way does each geometric change push the
result, how strongly, and why. Each model evaluates a closed triangulated body (or an ``Assembly`` of parts) face
by face, so a change in one part shows up in the mechanism and in the part it belongs to.

* ``ExternalFlow``: drag and lift of a body in a stream. Windward faces: modified Newtonian pressure
  ``Cp = Cp_stag sin^2(delta)``; leeward faces inclined less than the separation angle recover pressure, steeper ones
  are separated and see the base pressure; friction from the flat-plate skin-friction law on attached faces
  (Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic Drag*, 1965, ch. 3 and 6; Anderson, *Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics*, for
  the Newtonian law).
* ``ConvectiveCooling``: heat rejected by a body at uniform temperature: local flat-plate correlations from each
  part's leading edge (laminar 0.332 Re_x^0.5 Pr^(1/3), turbulent 0.0296 Re_x^0.8 Pr^(1/3)), reduced coefficient in
  separated regions, natural convection from the vertical-plate law, optional fin efficiency tanh(mL)/(mL)
  (Incropera & DeWitt, ch. 3, 7 and 9).
* ``Cantilever``: a body clamped at one end with a tip load: non-uniform Euler-Bernoulli beam with section
  properties from a voxelization, tip deflection, bending stress, mass and a Rayleigh estimate of the first
  frequency (Timoshenko & Gere; Rao, *Mechanical Vibrations*).
* ``ScalingModel``: any user formula of the descriptors (``pinneapple_design.qualitative.descriptors``).

The estimates are order-of-magnitude: they rank variants and explain trends; the numbers come from the quantitative
step (``QualitativePreview.quantify``).

classes.doc:
User formulas of the geometric descriptors, e.g. ``ScalingModel({"conduction_resistance": lambda d, c:
d.length / (c["k"] * d.frontal_area)}, better={"conduction_resistance": "min"}, k=200)``. The mechanisms are the
descriptors: each one's share of a change comes from swapping it alone (in log space).

methods.name: log_attribution
methods.doc: Share of ln(q_var / q_base) attributed to each descriptor (one-at-a-time swap from the baseline).

functions.name: sheltered_faces
functions.sig: (V: np.ndarray, F: np.ndarray, normals: np.ndarray, centroids: np.ndarray, direction, grid: int = 96, tol: float = 0.05) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Windward faces hidden behind other surfaces seen from upstream (in the wake of something in front of them):
the windward triangles are rasterized on the plane normal to the flow, keeping the most upstream depth per
cell; a windward face whose cell has a surface more than ``tol`` x body length upstream of it is sheltered.

children.summary: Cheap physical models that turn a geometry into first estimates, the mechanisms behind them and a surface map.

children.name: pinneapple_design.qualitative.preview
children.doc:
Qualitative preview: how each geometry, or each change to a part, should affect the result, before any
simulation; then the quantitative check.

>>> from pinneapple_design.qualitative import preview
>>> p = preview({"baseline": body, "longer tail": body2, "blunt rear": body3}, objective="minimizar arrasto",
...             conditions={"U": 30})
>>> print(p.text())                # direction, strength, mechanism and confidence for each variant
>>> p.figure("preview.png")        # surface maps (where the physics happens) and the expected changes
>>> check = p.quantify(lambda name, geom: run_cfd(geom))   # numbers only for the variants worth simulating

The preview is meant to be read first: it says *why* (the mechanisms that move the objective and by how much
relative to each other), flags side effects on the other quantities, and lowers its confidence where the cheap model
is known to be fragile (near a separation threshold, in the transition range, short beams, low fin efficiency...).
``quantify`` then compares those expectations with an accurate computation (CFD, FEM, ``pp.solve``, experiments) and
reports where the qualitative reading was right or wrong.

methods.name: to_simulate
methods.doc:
Variants worth the quantitative step first: the best expected ones, then the least certain among the
rest (where the qualitative reading could be wrong), always with the baseline.

methods.name: figure
methods.sig: (path: str | None = None, lang: str | None = None, max_faces: int = 6000, view: tuple[float, float] = (22, -125), same_scale: bool = True)
methods.doc:
Surface map of each variant (where the physics acts, same colour scale for all) and the expected change
of the objective split into mechanisms.

methods.name: quantify
methods.sig: (compute: Callable[[str, Any], float], variants: list[str] | None = None) -> QuantitativeCheck
methods.doc:
Run an accurate computation of the objective (``compute(name, geometry) -> value``: CFD, FEM, a
``pp.solve`` problem, an experiment) on ``variants`` (default ``to_simulate()``, always with the baseline) and
compare with the qualitative expectations: direction of each change, ranking, and where it was wrong.

methods.name: rank_correlation
methods.doc: Spearman correlation between the expected and the computed objective over the computed variants.

methods.name: text
methods.sig: (lang: str | None = None, top: int = 12) -> str

methods.name: figure
methods.sig: (path: str | None = None, lang: str | None = None)

``("tip_deflection", "min")``. ``conditions`` are the model's operating conditions (speed, temperature

functions.sig: (assembly: Assembly, objective: str | tuple | Objective, conditions: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, step: float = 0.2, model: QualitativeModel | str | None = None, lang: str = 'pt', axes: str = 'xyz', about: str = 'min') -> PartSensitivity

For each part: grow it by ``step`` along each axis (about its minimum corner by default, i.e. away from where

children.name: pinneapple_design.qualitative.quantitative
children.doc:
Quantitative counterparts of the qualitative models, for ``QualitativePreview.quantify``.

``voxel_fem_cantilever``: 3-D linear elasticity on the voxelized geometry (any shape: holes, flanges, tapers),
clamped at one end with a load spread over the other. Hexahedral elements with Wilson's incompatible modes
(Wilson, Taylor, Doherty & Ghaboussi 1973), whose three extra bubble modes per direction let a single element bend
without the shear locking of the plain trilinear brick; the bubbles are condensed out. It captures what beam theory
leaves out (shear deformation of short beams, stress concentration at section changes, flanges that do not work), so
it is the check for ``Cantilever`` previews.

functions.name: hex8_incompatible_stiffness
functions.sig: (size, E: float, nu: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: 24 x 24 stiffness of a rectangular brick ``size = (hx, hy, hz)`` with Wilson's incompatible modes condensed.

functions.name: voxel_fem_cantilever
functions.sig: (geom: Any, E: float = 70000000000.0, nu: float = 0.3, load: float = 1000.0, axis: int | None = None, load_axis: int = 2, clamp: str = 'min', n_slices: int = 40, cells_across: int = 8, rho: float = 2700.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Tip deflection, stiffness, maximum von Mises stress and mass of a body clamped at one end of ``axis`` (default
the longest) with ``load`` (N) along ``load_axis`` spread over the other end face. ``cells_across``: voxels along
the larger section dimension (the other is scaled to keep the voxels near cubic).

children.summary: Quantitative counterparts of the qualitative models, for QualitativePreview.quantify.

children.doc:
Qualitative physics preview of geometries and geometry changes, before the quantitative analysis.

Give it different geometries (or an ``Assembly`` whose parts you change) and a physical goal, and it tells you, from
cheap physical models, which way each geometry or change should push the result, how strongly, through which
mechanism, with what confidence, and where on the surface the physics acts; then ``quantify`` runs the accurate
computation only where it is worth it and checks the qualitative reading.

>>> from pinneapple_design.qualitative import preview, part_sensitivity, Assembly
>>> p = preview({"baseline": body, "rounded rear": body2}, "minimizar arrasto", {"U": 30})
>>> print(p.text()); p.figure("preview.png")
>>> part_sensitivity(Assembly({"base": plate, "fin_1": fin1, "fin_2": fin2}), "maximizar resfriamento").text()
