children.name: pinneapple_design.satellite
pinneapple_design.satellite.budgets
children.doc:
Closed-form budgets of a small Earth-observation satellite: orbit (sun-synchronous inclination, J2 drift, eclipse,
revisit), power (end-of-life array, battery depth of discharge), single-node thermal (hot and cold cases), RF link
(EIRP, path loss, G/T, Eb/N0) and the attitude disturbance torques with wheel and magnetorquer sizing.

The formulas are the standard ones of Wertz and Larson, *Space Mission Analysis and Design* (3rd ed., 1999):
power sizing with peak-power tracking (X_e = 0.60, X_d = 0.80, eq. 11-5), disturbance torques (table 11-9), the
momentum a wheel stores over a quarter orbit (0.707 T P / 4), the magnetorquer dipole ``T / B``. Component
properties (cell efficiency, battery energy density, catalogue-like wheel and torquer steps) are representative
values, not a vendor's data.

functions.name: nodal_rate
functions.sig: (a: float, e: float, i_rad: float) -> float
functions.doc: Secular J2 drift of the ascending node, rad/s: ``-3/2 n J2 (R_E / p)^2 cos i``.

functions.name: sso_inclination
functions.sig: (h_km: float, e: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc: Inclination (deg) whose J2 node drift equals the Sun's mean motion.

functions.name: eclipse_fraction
functions.sig: (h_km: float, beta_deg: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Fraction of a circular orbit in the Earth's cylindrical shadow:
``acos(sqrt(h^2 + 2 R h) / ((R + h) cos beta)) / pi`` for ``|beta| < asin(R / (R + h))``, else 0.

functions.name: eclipse_fraction_sampled
functions.sig: (h_km: float, beta_deg: float, n: int = 200000) -> float
functions.doc: The same fraction from geometry: points of the orbit behind the Earth (r . s < 0) within R_E of the Sun line.

functions.name: beta_angles_sso
functions.sig: (i_deg: float, ltan_h: float, n: int = 365) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Sun-orbit-plane angle over a year for a sun-synchronous orbit with local time of ascending node ``ltan_h``
(mean Sun; the equation of time, at most 16 min, is neglected): ``sin beta = cos d sin i sin(O - a) + sin d cos i``
with the node fixed relative to the mean Sun.

functions.name: revisit
functions.sig: (h_km: float, i_deg: float, fov_deg: float, ifov_urad: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Ground-track spacing at the equator, swath (flat Earth, nadir), the days to close the equatorial gap with
one pass per orbit (``spacing / swath``) and the ground sample distance ``h IFOV``.

functions.name: solar_array
functions.sig: (p_day_w: float, p_ecl_w: float, period_s: float, f_ecl: float, years: float, *, efficiency: float = 0.28, inherent_degradation: float = 0.77, incidence_deg: float = 23.5, degradation_per_year: float = 0.0275, kg_per_m2: float = 2.0, x_e: float = 0.6, x_d: float = 0.8) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Array power and area sized at end of life (SMAD eq. 11-5 to 11-8).

functions.name: battery
functions.sig: (p_ecl_w: float, period_s: float, f_ecl: float, years: float, *, eta: float = 0.9, wh_per_kg: float = 100.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Capacity from the eclipse energy at the depth of discharge the cycle count allows.

functions.name: surface
functions.sig: (coating: Coating, radiator_fraction: float) -> Coating
functions.doc:
Area-weighted optical properties of a box whose ``radiator_fraction`` of the surface carries ``coating`` and
the rest MLI (the single-node approximation of a radiator).

functions.name: thermal_cases
functions.sig: (dims_m: tuple[float, float, float], h_km: float, coating: Coating, q_int_hot: float, q_int_cold: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Single-node equilibrium of a box: hot = sunlit, subsolar albedo and Earth IR on the nadir face, full internal
power; cold = eclipse, Earth IR only, the least internal power. Area to the Sun: the largest face; to the Earth:
a face with view factor ``(R / (R + h))^2``. Radiates from its whole surface with the (effective) properties of
``coating`` (see :func:`surface`).

functions.name: slant_range
functions.sig: (h_km: float, elev_deg: float) -> float
functions.doc: Range (m) to a satellite at altitude ``h`` seen at elevation ``elev`` from the ground.

functions.name: link_budget
functions.sig: (*, p_tx_w: float, f_hz: float, h_km: float, elev_deg: float, g_tx_dbi: float, g_over_t_db_k: float, rate_bps: float, ebn0_req_db: float, line_loss_db: float = 1.0, atm_loss_db: float = 0.5, pol_loss_db: float = 0.5, point_loss_db: float = 1.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Downlink Eb/N0 and margin: ``EIRP - L_fs - L_other + G/T - 10 log k - 10 log R``.

functions.name: disturbance_torques
functions.sig: (*, h_km: float, rho_kg_m3: float, inertia: tuple[float, float, float], area_m2: float, cp_offset_m: float, residual_dipole_am2: float, deviation_deg: float = 10.0, cd: float = 2.2, reflectance: float = 0.6) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Worst-case torques (N m), SMAD table 11-9: gravity gradient, aerodynamic, solar pressure, magnetic (polar
field ``2 M / R^3``).

functions.name: wheel_and_torquer
functions.sig: (torque_nm: float, period_s: float, b_min_t: float, inertia: tuple[float, float, float], *, slew_deg: float = 30.0, slew_s: float = 60.0, margin: float = 2.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Wheel momentum ``0.707 T P / 4`` (cyclic disturbance over a quarter orbit) and slew torque ``4 theta I / t^2``,
each with ``margin``; torquer dipole ``margin T / B_min``. Three wheels and three torquers.

children.name: pinneapple_design.satellite.workflow
children.doc:
The standard satellite-design workflow (#1207): from the mission (ground sample distance, revisit, payload power
and data per day, lifetime) to the orbit, power, thermal, link and attitude budgets, the mass and power budget closed
at the least mass with margins, and an orbit propagation over the lifetime that re-verifies the margins.

1. **Orbit**: for each candidate altitude, the sun-synchronous inclination (J2 node drift = the Sun's mean motion),
   the beta angle over a year at the chosen local time of the node, the worst eclipse fraction, revisit and ground
   sample distance, the daily contact time with the ground station.
2. **Budgets** (:mod:`.budgets`): the solar array at end of life with degradation, the battery at the depth of
   discharge the cycle count allows, the coating and heater that keep the single node within its limits in the hot
   and cold cases, the data rate and transmitter power that close the link with margin, the disturbance torques
   (gravity gradient, drag at high solar flux, solar pressure, magnetic) with wheel and magnetorquer sizing.
3. **Lifetime**: orbit decay (:func:`pinneapple_physics.astro.decay.reference_decay`, NRLMSIS 2.0 when ``pymsis``
   is installed) for low, mean and high F10.7: the mission must survive the high-flux scenario and re-enter within
   the disposal limit in the low-flux one.
4. **Design**: the mass closed by fixed point (structure and harness as fractions, system margin), the least mass
   over the candidate altitudes that meets every constraint.
5. **Re-verification**: a Cowell J2 propagation (node drift and eclipse fraction measured on the trajectory), the
   decay to the end of life, and at the end-of-life altitude the power (battery state of charge stepped over the
   orbits), thermal (transient node bounded by the steady cases) and pointing margins (wheel momentum, torquer
   authority against the end-of-life drag).

children.name: pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse
pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.brake_rotor
children.doc:
Vented brake rotor: the radial vanes between the two friction rings, as a fin array, under a sustained load.

Ground truth: the same 1-D fin-array formula as :mod:`.heatsink_fins` (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.
fin_array_conduction`) with cast iron (``k = 50 W/m K``) and rotor-scale geometry: the vanes are fins of length =
vent gap spread along the mean circumference, the friction ring is the base (extended-surface analysis of vented
rotor cooling: e.g. Limpert, *Brake Design and Safety*). Lumped and steady: a uniform convection coefficient per
driving profile and a sustained heat input (a long descent), not a single hard stop (that is a transient problem; see
the ``car_brake_thermal`` PDE preset). The temperature rise is linear in power, so the surrogate learns the thermal
resistance.

The analysis of its own: :func:`monte_carlo_uncertainty` propagates machining tolerances on vane thickness and gap
through the formula (:func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate`, uniform within the band) and grades
the 95th-percentile temperature against the safe limit.

functions.name: profile_params
functions.sig: (design: RotorDesign, power_w: float, h_conv: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Formula quantities, plus ``theta_vane_base_c`` (alias of the fin-root rise) and ``lc_radial_m`` (corrected
length along the vane's radial extent, for the radial colour profile).

functions.name: rotor_temperature_c
functions.sig: (design: RotorDesign, power_w: float, h_conv: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Ground truth: friction-ring temperature under a sustained heat input.

Returns
-------
T : float [degC]
    Friction-ring temperature.

functions.name: thermal_resistance_k_w
functions.sig: (design: RotorDesign, h_conv: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Thermal resistance from the friction ring to the air.

Returns
-------
R : float [K/W]
    Thermal resistance.

functions.name: vane_temperature_at_radial_position_c
functions.sig: (design: RotorDesign, power_w: float, h_conv: float, r_fraction: float) -> float
functions.doc:
The fin profile (same ``m`` and root rise) along the vane's radial extent: hottest at the inner edge
(``r_fraction = 0``), coolest at the outer edge. Used to colour the vanes; the scalar model integrates over the
gap direction, this profile is a display of the same fin parameters along the radius.

Returns
-------
T : float [degC]
    Vane temperature at ``r_fraction``.

functions.sig: (design: RotorDesign, power_w: float, h_conv: float, safety_threshold_c: float, n_samples: int = 200, seed: int | None = None, thickness_tolerance_m: float = VANE_THICKNESS_TOLERANCE_M, gap_tolerance_m: float = VANE_GAP_TOLERANCE_M) -> dict

children.name: pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.core
children.doc:
The machinery shared by every case: a small MLP surrogate, gradient descent on the design through the frozen
surrogate, and a verification card that re-checks the answer against the ground truth.

The method (also called "backprop into the design"): sample the design space, label every sample with the ground
truth model, train an MLP on those labels, freeze its weights and treat the design variables as the only trainable
tensor. The surrogate is differentiable, so Adam can move the design along the gradient of the predicted objective
plus constraint penalties. The surrogate's answer is never reported on its own say-so: :class:`VerificationCard`
re-runs the ground truth on the final design and grades the gap.

classes.name: MLPSurrogate
classes.sig: (bounds: Sequence[tuple[float, float]], hidden: int = 48, n_layers: int = 3, log_output: bool = False)
classes.doc:
``tanh`` MLP with its inputs mapped from their bounds to [-1, 1] and its output standardised.

``log_output=True`` fits ``log(y)``: right for a positive output that spans orders of magnitude (a thermal
resistance, a release rate, a stress) and keeps the prediction positive. ``forward`` takes and returns physical
units, so the frozen surrogate can sit inside a loss written in physical units.

classes.name: SurrogateFit
classes.doc:
A trained surrogate with its held-out errors (relative, on rows it never trained on).

Attributes
----------
val_mean_rel_err : float [-]
    Mean relative error on held-out rows.
val_p95_rel_err : float [-]
    95th percentile.
val_max_rel_err : float [-]
    Largest.
n_train : int [-]
    Training rows.
n_val : int [-]
    Held-out rows.
epochs : int [-]
    Epochs.
seconds : float [s]
    Training time.

classes.name: VerificationCard
classes.doc:
The final design re-checked against the ground truth (never the surrogate grading itself).

``covered`` and ``not_covered`` name what this card does and does not check, so its coverage is explicit:
``len(covered) / (len(covered) + len(not_covered))``. ``values`` holds the case's numbers (real and surrogate
outputs, errors).

methods.name: trust_report
methods.doc:
The same checks as a :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport` (FAIL is critical, WARNING is a
non-critical contradiction), with every ``not_covered`` item as a check that did not run.

functions.name: fit_surrogate
functions.sig: (X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor, bounds: Sequence[tuple[float, float]], *, hidden: int = 48, n_layers: int = 3, epochs: int = 1500, lr: float = 0.003, seed: int = 0, log_output: bool = False, val_fraction: float = 0.1, rel_floor: float = 1e-12) -> SurrogateFit
functions.doc:
Full-batch Adam with a cosine learning-rate decay on ``(X, y)``; the last ``val_fraction`` of the rows (the
data are expected in random order) is held out and scored as ``|pred - y| / max(|y|, rel_floor)``.

functions.name: freeze
functions.sig: (model: nn.Module) -> nn.Module
functions.doc: Stop gradients into the weights: from here on only the design moves.

functions.name: descend
functions.sig: (loss_fn: Callable[[dict[str, torch.Tensor]], torch.Tensor], x0: Mapping[str, float], *, bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], steps: int = 400, lr: float | Mapping[str, float] = 0.01, reparam: str = 'clamp', project: Callable[[dict[str, torch.Tensor]], None] | None = None) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Adam on the design variables ``x0`` to minimise ``loss_fn(values)``.

``reparam="clamp"`` optimises the physical values and clamps them to ``bounds`` after every step, then calls
``project(values)`` (in place, without gradients) for constraints that couple variables. ``reparam="sigmoid"``
optimises an unconstrained tensor per variable mapped through ``low + (high - low) * sigmoid(raw)``, which puts
variables of very different magnitude on the same footing (one learning rate moves all of them).

functions.name: banded
functions.sig: (name: str, error: float, pass_limit: float, warn_limit: float, *, pass_text: str, warn_text: str, fail_text: str) -> CheckResult
functions.doc: PASS when ``error <= pass_limit``, WARNING up to ``warn_limit``, FAIL above.

functions.name: relative_error
functions.sig: (predicted: float, reference: float, floor: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Relative error of ``predicted`` against ``reference``, with ``floor`` guarding a reference near zero.

Returns
-------
err : float [-]
    ``|predicted - reference| / max(|reference|, floor)``.

functions.name: constraint_checks
functions.sig: (violations: Mapping[str, float], ok_text: str = 'Within physical/manufacturing limit.', skip: Sequence[str] = ()) -> list[CheckResult]
functions.doc: One check per signed violation (``<= 0`` is satisfied).

children.name: pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.heatsink_fins
children.doc:
Straight-fin CPU heat sink: fin count, height and thickness on a fixed 80 x 80 mm aluminium base.

Ground truth: the 1-D fin-array formula (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.fin_array_conduction`, Incropera &
DeWitt fin efficiency with an adiabatic-tip correction, convective plus 1-D base resistance) with a prescribed
convection coefficient per fan profile. ``k = 205 W/m K`` is the aluminium value of the ``cpu_heatsink_thermal``
preset. The formula's temperature rise is linear in power, ``T_j = T_amb + P * R(N, H, t, h)``, so the surrogate
learns the thermal resistance ``R`` (in log scale) and the power enters exactly.

Independent check of the formula itself: :func:`fin_cell_check` solves 2-D finite-volume conduction in one fin pitch
(:mod:`pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_cell`).

Scope: a fixed convection coefficient (no airflow solve, no fin-to-fin flow interaction), steady state, no
measurement. For plate-fin sizing with published forced / natural convection correlations, pressure drop and a 3-D
base-plate solve use :mod:`pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink` (the HeatSink Sizer app) instead.

classes.doc:
A fin array on the fixed base.

functions.sig: (n_samples: int = 6000, epochs: int = 1500, seed: int = 0) -> SurrogateFit
functions.doc: MLP on ``log R``; ``fit.val_mean_rel_err`` is the held-out error on ``R``, i.e. on the temperature rise.

functions.sig: (surrogate, design: HeatsinkDesign, power_w: float, h_conv: float) -> float

functions.name: optimize_design
functions.sig: (surrogate, power_w: float, h_conv: float, steps: int = 400, lr: float = 0.05, penalty_weight: float = 100.0) -> OptimizationResult
functions.doc:
Minimise the surrogate's junction temperature over (N, H, t) from the baseline.

The loss is ``log R + penalty_weight * (relative spacing shortfall)^2`` (``T_j - T_amb = P R``, so the power
only scales the objective), descended in the sigmoid-bounded space of :func:`.core.descend`: N (tens), H
(centimetres) and t (tenths of a millimetre) move at comparable rates and stay inside their bounds. The final N
is rounded and stepped down until the integer design keeps the spacing rule (the coupled rule
``N <= (W + s_min) / (t + s_min)`` is not kept by bounding N and t separately).

children.name: pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.meshes

Triangle meshes of the five designs, in millimetres, for a 3-D viewer or an STL download.

Each part is a set of individually closed bodies (``pinneapple_design.geometry.bodies``) concatenated, not a boolean
union: the fins of a heat sink or the vanes of a rotor touch their base without being fused into one manifold. That
is right for display and for a slicer that accepts several shells; a CNC or FEM pipeline that needs one watertight
body has to fuse them (for example with ``manifold3d``).

children.name: pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.reflex_port
children.doc:
Bass-reflex port: radius and length that tune a cabinet to a target frequency, and the trade-off between a small
port and an accurate tuning.

Ground truth: the Helmholtz resonator (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.helmholtz_resonator`),
``f = c / (2 pi) sqrt(A / (V L_eff))`` with ``A = pi r^2`` and ``L_eff = L + 1.7 r`` (end correction of a port
flanged at both ends). Lumped: the air in the port moves as one mass, which holds while the port is short against the
wavelength; no cabinet modes, no port compression or air-speed limits, no driver model.

The analysis of its own: :func:`sweep_pareto_frontier` minimises
``lambda * volume_fraction + (1 - lambda) * rel_freq_error^2`` for a sweep of ``lambda``, where ``volume_fraction``
is the port volume over the largest port this case allows (6 % of the cabinet). Each weight starts gradient descent
from several points and keeps the candidate with the lowest loss evaluated with the closed form, not the surrogate.

functions.name: resonant_frequency_hz
functions.sig: (design: PortDesign, cabinet_volume_l: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Ground truth (training labels and verification).

Returns
-------
f : float [Hz]
    Port resonance.

functions.name: acoustic_field
functions.sig: (design: PortDesign, cabinet_volume_l: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: One value per design (the lumped model has no field along the port): the tuning within the target range.

functions.name: constraint_violations
functions.sig: (design: PortDesign, cabinet_volume_l: float) -> dict[str, float]

functions.name: design_to_dict
functions.sig: (design: PortDesign) -> dict

functions.name: generate_dataset
functions.sig: (n_samples: int, seed: int = 0) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]

functions.name: train_surrogate
functions.sig: (n_samples: int = 6000, epochs: int = 1500, seed: int = 0) -> SurrogateFit

functions.name: predict_frequency_hz
functions.sig: (surrogate, design: PortDesign, cabinet_volume_l: float) -> float

functions.name: optimize_design
functions.sig: (surrogate, cabinet_volume_l: float, target_freq_hz: float, steps: int = 400, lr: float = 0.05, penalty_weight: float = 100.0) -> OptimizationResult
functions.doc:
Minimise ``((f_surrogate - f_target) / f_target)^2`` plus a penalty on the port-volume rule, from the baseline,
in the sigmoid-bounded space of :func:`.core.descend` (radius and length bounded, comparable step sizes).

functions.name: sweep_pareto_frontier
functions.sig: (surrogate, cabinet_volume_l: float, target_freq_hz: float, n_points: int = 8, steps: int = 400, lr: float = 0.05, penalty_weight: float = 100.0) -> list[FrontierPoint]
functions.doc:
Volume-vs-accuracy trade-off for ``lambda`` in ``linspace(0.05, 0.95, n_points)``.

Per weight, descent starts from the previous weight's best design, the baseline and both corners of the bounds;
then every design found (plus the target-only optimum) competes for every weight and the lowest closed-form loss
wins. Selection by the closed form matters: descent towards small ports ends where the surrogate is less accurate
than its average and reports designs as on target that the formula puts several per cent off. The frontier can
still jump between adjacent weights (non-convex loss); every reported frequency and volume is from the formula.

functions.name: verify_design
functions.sig: (design: PortDesign, cabinet_volume_l: float, target_freq_hz: float, surrogate_predicted_freq_hz: float) -> VerificationCard

functions.name: mesh
functions.sig: (design: PortDesign) -> meshes.Mesh
functions.doc: Port tube with its flange, in millimetres.

functions.name: export_stl_bytes
functions.sig: (design: PortDesign) -> bytes

children.name: pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.suspension_arm
children.doc:
Suspension arm as a rectangular cantilever: the lightest width x thickness that still reaches a fatigue life.

Ground truth (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.cantilever_fatigue`, e.g. Shigley, *Mechanical Engineering
Design*): root bending stress ``sigma = 6 F L / (w t^2)`` and Basquin's stress-life law ``sigma_a = sigma_f' (2N)^b``.
The life target is turned into an allowable stress (``sigma_allow = sigma_f' (2 N_target)^b``), which is how the
problem is posed in practice and is far better conditioned than cycles, which span orders of magnitude. The material
constants are typical table values for a spring steel (``sigma_f' = 1200 MPa``, ``b = -0.09``), not a measured
material. No endurance limit (the power law keeps extrapolating at low stress), no stress concentrations (holes,
fillets), a constant section, one load case.

The analysis of its own: :func:`compute_sensitivity`, local derivatives of life and mass by central differences on
the closed form (:func:`pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.local_derivatives`) and their elasticities
``(x / f) df/dx``. For this model the life is a pure power law, ``N ~ w^(-1/b) t^(-2/b)``, so the elasticities are
exactly ``-1/b`` and ``-2/b``: thickness always matters twice as much as width.

classes.doc:

    Cycles to failure.

    Cycles per metre of width.
d_life_d_thickness : float [1/m]
    Cycles per metre of thickness.
d_mass_d_width : float [kg/m]
d_mass_d_thickness : float [kg/m]
elasticity_width : float [-]
    Relative change of life over relative change of width.
elasticity_thickness : float [-]
elasticity_ratio : float [-]
    Larger over smaller elasticity.

children.name: pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.transdermal_patch
children.doc:
Membrane-controlled release patch: area, membrane thickness and reservoir concentration for a target release rate
and wear time, with the smallest area.

Ground truth: Fick's first law through a rate-limiting membrane (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.
membrane_diffusion`, the reservoir-type delivery model of Robinson & Lee, *Controlled Drug Delivery*):
``rate = D K C_res A / L``, reservoir mass ``M = C_res A L_res``, depletion time ``t_dep = L_res L / (D K)``. The
depletion time depends on the membrane thickness only (area and concentration cancel), so the wear-time constraint is
applied through the closed form and the surrogate learns the rate.

``D`` and ``K`` are generic order-of-magnitude values for a small solute in a polymer membrane, not the measured
coefficients of any drug, and the model is a steady 1-D membrane with sink conditions at the outer face (no skin
resistance, no saturation plateau). This is a mass-transfer design exercise, not a dosing or medical tool.

The analysis of its own: :func:`simulate_release_timeseries`, the release over the wear time (constant zero-order
phase, then a first-order tail once the reservoir is depleted).

functions.name: release_rate_mg_day
functions.sig: (design: PatchDesign) -> float
functions.doc:
Ground truth: steady release rate (training labels and verification).

Returns
-------
rate : float [mg/day]
    Steady release rate.

functions.name: depletion_time_days
functions.sig: (design: PatchDesign) -> float
functions.doc:
Time to deplete the reservoir at the steady rate.

Returns
-------
t : float [day]
    Time to deplete the reservoir.

functions.name: reservoir_mass_mg
functions.sig: (design: PatchDesign) -> float
functions.doc:
Drug mass in the reservoir.

Returns
-------
m : float [mg]
    Drug mass in the reservoir.

functions.name: concentration_at_membrane_depth
functions.sig: (design: PatchDesign, z_from_reservoir_m: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Linear steady profile ``C(z) = K C_res (1 - z / L)`` (sink at the outer face).

Returns
-------
C : float [kg/m3]
    Concentration at ``z_from_reservoir_m``.

functions.name: decay_rate_constant_per_day
functions.sig: (design: PatchDesign) -> float
functions.doc:
First-order constant of the tail after depletion, ``k = D K / (L L_res) = 1 / t_dep`` (area cancels).

Returns
-------
k : float [1/day]
    First-order decay constant.

functions.name: simulate_release_timeseries
functions.sig: (design: PatchDesign, duration_days: float | None = None, n_points: int = 100) -> list[dict[str, float]]
functions.doc:
Rate, cumulative release and nominal reservoir left over time (default: 1.5 x the depletion time).

The tail treats the drug still dissolved at depletion as decaying with the steady transport constant; it does not
track a separate residual mass, so the cumulative release can exceed the nominal reservoir by a bounded amount
(about 39 % over a tail of half the depletion time).

functions.sig: (n_samples: int = 6000, epochs: int = 1500, seed: int = 0) -> SurrogateFit
functions.doc: MLP on ``log rate`` (the rate spans about 0.5 to 2600 mg/day over the design space).

functions.sig: (surrogate, design: PatchDesign) -> float

functions.sig: (surrogate, target_rate_mg_day: float, target_wear_days: float, steps: int = 1200, lr: float = 0.15, weight_rate: float = 80.0, weight_wear: float = 300.0) -> OptimizationResult

children.doc:
Surrogate-driven inverse design on closed-form physics, with the answer re-checked against the physics.

Five worked cases share one method (:mod:`.core`): sample the design space, label it with a closed-form model from
:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form`, train a small MLP, freeze it, run Adam on the design variables through it, and
grade the final design against the closed form (:class:`.core.VerificationCard`, also as a
:class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`). Each case adds one analysis of its own:

=====================  =========================================================  ===================================
module                 design                                                     extra analysis
=====================  =========================================================  ===================================
``heatsink_fins``      straight-fin heat sink (fin count, height, thickness)      2-D finite-volume fin-cell check
``brake_rotor``        vented brake rotor vanes (count, gap, thickness)           Monte Carlo of machining tolerances
``transdermal_patch``  membrane-controlled patch (area, membrane, concentration)  release over the wear time
``suspension_arm``     rectangular cantilever arm (width, thickness), min. mass   local sensitivities (elasticities)
``reflex_port``        bass-reflex port (radius, length) for a tuning frequency   volume-vs-accuracy trade-off sweep
=====================  =========================================================  ===================================

Each case module also builds its part as a triangle mesh in millimetres (:mod:`.meshes`) for a viewer or STL file.
The models are textbook closed forms with stated assumptions (each module docstring); none is validated against
measurements. The apps ``apps/heatsink_design_ai``, ``apps/brakecool_ai``, ``apps/patchdose_ai``,
``apps/ridetune_ai`` and ``apps/soundshape_ai`` serve them.
children.summary: Surrogate-driven inverse design on closed-form physics, with the answer re-checked against the physics.

    run = run_mission(DEFAULT_TEXT, out_dir="out")           # deterministic planner, no API key needed

with its arguments, a summary of its result and its wall time (:mod:`pinneapple_autolab.core`).

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling.learn
children.doc:
Fast approximation of the coupled reference: junction temperatures and the board-top temperature field.

Two parametric reduced-order models (:class:`pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.ParametricPOD`, POD + one
Gaussian process per coefficient) on ``log(T - T_air)``:

* the junction temperatures of every part, nominal and pessimistic (:func:`.simulate.response`);
* the board-top map (POD of the snapshots, ``MAP_SHAPE`` grid).

The Gaussian processes give a predictive standard deviation, carried back to °C (delta method) so the optimiser can
ask for the limit to hold at ``mean + k std`` and the trust report can check that the stated spread covers the
measured hold-out errors. :func:`holdout` measures it on designs the model never saw, against the nearest-snapshot
baseline every surrogate must beat.

methods.sig: (X: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray, maps: np.ndarray) -> CoolingSurrogate

methods.name: predict
methods.sig: (X: np.ndarray, maps: bool = True) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
methods.doc: Junction temperatures (n, n_out) with their std [K]; with ``maps`` the board-top map (n, ny, nx) too.

functions.name: errors
functions.sig: (pred_tj, pred_map, Y, maps) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: holdout
functions.sig: (data: dict[str, np.ndarray], t_air_c: float, *, test_fraction: float = 0.2, seed: int = 0, modes: int = 16) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Train on part of the reference solves, measure on the rest: errors of the surrogate and of the nearest
snapshot, coverage of the +-2 std band, prediction time against the reference time.

children.summary: Fast approximation of the coupled reference: junction temperatures and the board-top temperature field.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling.mission
children.doc:
The cooling mission: a board with an overheating part, the limits, the space, the fan budget, the design space.

    m = default_mission()                       # 160 x 100 mm 4-layer board, 30 W SoC in a 35 x 35 BGA, 35 °C air
    m = parse_mission("SoC de 30 W ... Tj max 95 °C ... dissipador até 70 x 70 x 30 mm ... ventoinha 0.05 W")
    m.space.sample(n, rng)                      # Latin hypercube designs inside the space, geometrically feasible

Every value parsed from the text keeps the words it came from (``m.provenance``); values not in the text are the
defaults of :func:`default_mission` and are listed as such.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling.optimize
children.doc:
Constrained search on the surrogate, verification on the reference, and the loop between them.

:func:`optimize`: lightest heat sink (mass from the closed form, exact) whose every part meets its junction limit
with pessimistic cooling at ``mean + k std`` of the surrogate, whose fan air power stays inside the budget and whose
fins keep the minimum gap; differential evolution with the fin count as an integer (``scipy.optimize``).

:func:`design_loop`: fit -> optimise -> run the reference on the optimum -> add it to the snapshots -> refit, until
the reference confirms the optimum (it meets every limit and lies inside the surrogate's +-2 std band) or the
rounds run out. Every round is kept (prediction, reference, error), so the evolution of the maximum temperature is a
measured history, not a story.

functions.sig: (mission: CoolingMission, X: np.ndarray, tj_upper: np.ndarray, fan_w: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Sum of the positive parts of every constraint, each scaled to a comparable size (1 = 1 K, 10 % of the fan
budget, 0.1 mm of fin gap). ``tj_upper``: (n, n_parts) pessimistic junction temperatures to hold.

functions.sig: (mission: CoolingMission, sur: CoolingSurrogate, *, k_sigma: float = 2.0, seed: int = 0, maxiter: int = 120, popsize: int = 24) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Minimum-mass design on the surrogate. Returns the design, its prediction and the per-generation history of
the best member (mass, predicted pessimistic hot-part temperature, violation).

Learn -> optimise -> verify on the reference -> add the verified point, until confirmed. ``data``: the
output of :func:`.simulate.simulate_many` (extended in place with the verified points).

children.summary: Constrained search on the surrogate, verification on the reference, and the loop between them.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling.scene
children.doc:
3-D scene of the cooled board: enclosure, fans, board temperature map, parts, heat sink and the warm air.

Everything coloured comes from a solve:

* board top: the board-top map of :func:`.simulate.simulate` (``MAP_SHAPE``), on jet;
* parts: their junction temperature;
* heat sink: base from the 3D finite-volume base solve (its top face), fins from the 1D fin equation from the local
  root temperature (``field3d`` of :func:`pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.evaluate_design`);
* air paths (forced convection only): straight paths along the flow from the fans, each coloured by the bulk
  temperature of its strip of air from an energy balance (heat from the board-top cells under the strip, and from the
  heat sink for strips through the fins, over ``rho cp V A`` of the strip). Paths do not mix sideways; they show where
  the heat goes, they are not a CFD solution.

:func:`timeline_scene` animates a sequence of states (bare board, still-air heat sink, the design rounds, the verified
design) on one geometry: the heat sink has room for the largest fin count of the sequence and unused fins collapse
to a point, so the vertex count stays fixed across frames.

Centres (x, y, z) of the three fans on the inlet wall and their radius [mm].

to a point on the base). ``design`` None: everything collapsed (no heat sink).

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling.simulate
children.doc:
Reference simulation of a cooled board: the 3D board model and the heat sink model, coupled.

* Board: :func:`pinneapple_physics.pcb.solve` (layered 3D finite volumes, JEDEC two-resistor packages, convection +
  radiation from both faces at the fan air speed).
* Heat sink on the hot part: :func:`pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.evaluate_design` (3D finite-volume base,
  fin correlations, pressure drop) gives the case-to-air resistance ``R = (T_source - T_air) / Q`` (interface
  material + spreading + fins) for the heat ``Q`` that actually goes up through the case.
* Coupling: ``Q`` depends on ``R`` (the rest goes into the board) and, in still air, ``R`` depends on ``Q``; the two
  are iterated to a fixed point (relative change of ``Q`` below ``tol``).

``simulate(..., pessimistic=True)`` repeats the coupled solve with the convection band of both models (board surface
coefficients x 0.8, heat-sink coefficient x 0.85: the H_BAND of each engine, typical correlation accuracy) so a design
can be required to meet its limits even with pessimistic cooling.

Board-top temperatures are returned on a fixed grid (``MAP_SHAPE``) whatever the solver grid, so solutions of
different fidelity can be compared point by point and used as snapshots of a field surrogate.

functions.sig: (board) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: (y, x) cell centres of MAP_SHAPE in mm.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling.verify
children.doc:
Independent verification of the chosen design and its trust report.

The design the loop confirmed is solved again with both models on finer grids (``FIDELITY["verify"]``: board cells
x2 in each direction, heat-sink base grid x2), so the decision does not rest on the grid the surrogate was trained
on. The trust report (:class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`) collects:

* limits: every junction at or below its limit with pessimistic cooling (critical), fan air power within budget
  (critical), heat sink inside the envelope (critical);
* physics: board energy balance, coupling fixed point converged, the heat-sink engine's own checks (energy balance,
  spreading by two methods, grid convergence, correlation range), grid convergence of the coupled solve
  (train vs verify grid);
* the surrogate: its prediction of the design within its +-2 std band of the fine solve plus the grid difference,
  hold-out error and coverage measured on unseen designs, applicability (inside the design space, no farther from
  a snapshot than the held-out designs whose error was measured).

functions.sig: (mission: CoolingMission, design: CoolingDesign, *, coarse: dict[str, Any] | None = None, prediction: dict[str, np.ndarray] | None = None, holdout: dict[str, Any] | None = None, train_X: np.ndarray | None = None, test_X: np.ndarray | None = None, fidelity: str | dict = 'verify') -> dict[str, Any]

children.summary: Independent verification of the chosen design and its trust report.

children.doc:
The self-optimizing engineer: cool an overheating part on a board with a heat sink and the enclosure fans.

    from pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling import run_mission, DEFAULT_TEXT
    run = run_mission(DEFAULT_TEXT, out_dir="out")       # read -> baseline -> still air -> sample -> learn ->
                                                         # optimise + confirm -> verify -> deliver

Modules: ``mission`` (request, design space), ``simulate`` (coupled 3-D board + heat sink reference), ``learn``
(POD + Gaussian-process surrogate of the junction temperatures and the board map, hold-out), ``optimize`` (constrained
search, confirm-on-physics loop), ``verify`` (fine-grid solve, trust report), ``scene`` (3-D), ``report``
(figures, renders, report), ``agent`` (controlled tools and planners).
children.summary: The self-optimizing engineer: cool an overheating part on a board with a heat sink and the enclosure fans.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_array_speed
children.doc:
How much faster is a trained surrogate than a numerical solve, and how far apart are they? A measured sweep over
seven plate-fin heat sinks.

The heat sink, its closed form and its surrogate are those of
:mod:`pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.heatsink_fins` (80 x 80 mm aluminium base, 3 mm thick, straight fins,
uniform film coefficient; MLP on the thermal resistance, trained on the fin-array formula of
:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.fin_array_conduction`). The numerical reference is the finite-volume fin pitch
of :func:`pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_cell.solve_fin_cell` (2-D cross-section, which is the same problem as the
3-D periodic cell because nothing depends on the fin depth), with its grid-halving check.

For each design the surrogate forward pass is timed (mean of ``timing_reps`` calls after one warm-up call) and the
reference solve is timed (wall clock, including its grid check), and the agreement is the difference of the
temperature rise above ambient, ``|dT_surrogate - dT_ref| / dT_ref``. The speed ratio depends on the machine and on
the reference solver: this reference is a sub-second 2-D solve, so the ratios are much smaller than against a meshed
3-D FEM run.

The seven designs stay at 55 W or more and inside the manufacturable box of ``heatsink_fins``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_cell
children.doc:
Finite-volume conduction in one fin pitch of a straight-fin heat sink: an independent check of the 1-D fin-array
formula (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.fin_array_conduction`).

The unit cell is one fin of thickness ``t`` and height ``H`` centred on a strip of base plate one pitch wide
(``pitch = spacing + t``) and ``t_base`` thick, the same cell a 3-D FEM check of a periodic fin array uses:

* bottom face: uniform heat flux, this fin's share of the power, ``q = P / (N * pitch * depth)``;
* exposed base top, fin sides and fin tip: convection ``-k dT/dn = h (T - T_amb)`` (Robin) with the same ``h`` as
  the formula;
* the two side planes ``x = 0`` and ``x = pitch``: symmetry with the neighbouring cells (zero flux);
* the two end planes along the depth: zero flux (the periodic simplification), with ``q`` and ``h`` uniform along
  the depth.

With nothing varying along the depth, the 3-D problem is exactly this 2-D cross-section problem (per unit depth),
which is what is solved here: cell-centred finite volumes on a grid that puts cell faces on the fin walls and the
fin root, two-point fluxes between cell centres (one material), half-cell resistances in series with ``1/h`` on convective
faces, and a direct sparse solve. Unlike the formula it resolves two-dimensional conduction in the fin (no 1-D fin
assumption, no corrected-length tip) and the spreading from the base into the fin root.

The result reports the energy balance (convected heat / applied heat) and, with ``refine=True``, the change of the
junction temperature rise when the grid is halved (a grid-convergence check).

n_cells : int [-]

    Relative change of the rise on a grid twice as fine.

pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.engine
children.doc:
Physics engine of the HeatSink Sizer: evaluates one design, fully verified.

Every number returned here comes from physics, not from the neural
surrogate: the closed-form network in
``pinneapple_physics.closed_form.plate_fin_heatsink`` (convection
correlations, fin efficiency, pressure drop) plus a 3D finite-volume solve
of the base (hotspot + temperature map). The two methods cross-check each
other, and each check is reported with a pass/warn/fail status.

functions.sig: (g: HeatSinkGeometry, op: OperatingInput, r_conv: float, n: int = 40) -> Dict[str, Any]

functions.name: physics_resistance
functions.sig: (design: DesignInput, op: OperatingInput, n: int = 36) -> Dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Base-to-ambient resistance (no TIM) from the FVM-resolved hotspot, plus
pressure drop -- the quantity the surrogate is trained to reproduce.

functions.sig: (g: HeatSinkGeometry, op: OperatingInput, fvm: Dict[str, Any], nominal: Dict[str, Any], t_amb: float, max_cells: int = 64, n_z: int = 14) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Surface temperatures of the whole heat sink for the 3D viewer.

* Base: bottom and top faces straight from the 3D finite-volume solve.
* Fins: each fin root takes the local top-face temperature under it
  (along the flow direction), and the temperature up the fin follows
  the 1D fin equation used by the resistance network,
  theta(z)/theta_root = cosh(m (Lc - z)) / cosh(m Lc)
  (Incropera, adiabatic tip via the corrected length Lc).
All lengths in mm, temperatures in °C.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.field
children.doc:
3D finite-volume conduction solve of the heat-sink base plate.

Independent of the closed-form spreading formula: it resolves the actual
rectangular source footprint (and an off-centre position) on the actual
rectangular base, so it both produces the temperature map shown to the
user and cross-checks :func:`spreading_resistance` (Lee et al.).

Model (same assumptions as the resistance network):
* bottom face: uniform heat flux Q/A_source over the footprint, adiabatic
  elsewhere; side faces adiabatic;
* top face: fins + exposed base lumped into a uniform effective
  coefficient ``h_eff = 1 / (R_fins * A_base)`` to ambient.

The linear system is assembled on cell centres (in-plane cell count held
roughly constant across aspect ratios) and solved directly (scipy.sparse); the energy balance (heat out through the top = Q) is
reported as a check.

functions.sig: (*, base_width: float, base_depth: float, base_thickness: float, k: float, power_w: float, r_fins_k_w: float, source_width: float, source_depth: float, source_x: Optional[float] = None, source_y: Optional[float] = None, nx: int = 48, ny: int = 48, nz: Optional[int] = None) -> Dict[str, object]

children.summary: 3D finite-volume conduction solve of the heat-sink base plate.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.monotone
children.doc:
Heat-sink surrogate trained with monotonicity constraints (zoo model ``heatsink_natural_mlp``).

The app's unconstrained natural-convection surrogate fits the physics engine to 0.7 % but gets the sign of the
conductivity effect wrong on 5 % of held-out designs: raising k by 5 % lowers the engine's resistance by only 0.13 %
(median over 400 designs), below the fit error, so a plain regression does not resolve it. :func:`train_monotone`
trains the same architecture (``bench_mlp`` 4 x 128 SiLU, same features, same split) with a hinge penalty
(:func:`pinneapple_neural.trainer.monotonic.monotonicity_penalty`) on d log R / d log k and d log R / d log(source
width), both required to be <= -``MARGIN``, evaluated on the training designs and on random in-range designs: the
library ``Trainer`` (Adam, best-val checkpoint; plain regression for ``WARMUP`` epochs, then the constrained
objective), then a full-batch L-BFGS polish of the same objective (``multi_round_lbfgs``).

Power is not constrained: the engine's own resistance rises with power on 0.5 % of designs (up to +0.7 % for a +5 %
step), so "more power, lower resistance" is not a law of the reference.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.sizer
children.doc:
Sizing: requirements in, verified heat-sink designs out.

1. Sample tens of thousands of manufacturable candidates inside the
   customer's envelope and process rules.
2. Screen them: with the PINNeAPPle surrogate (FVM-accurate, microseconds
   per design) when the request is inside its trained design space, else
   with the closed-form network (vectorised loop, still fast). The screen
   uses the surrogate's conformal 95% upper bound, so it errs on the safe
   side.
3. Round the best candidates to manufacturing precision and re-verify each
   one with the full physics engine (FVM base + pessimistic convection
   band). Only verified designs are recommended.

children.name: pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.surrogate
children.doc:
Neural surrogate of the physics engine, used only to *screen* designs.

The finite-volume-resolved physics takes ~40 ms per design; the sizer
needs to screen tens of thousands of candidates per request. A PINNeAPPle
MLP (``ModelRegistry`` + ``Trainer`` + L-BFGS finetune) learns the
base-to-ambient resistance (and pressure drop) over the design space, and
every design it proposes is then re-verified by the physics engine before
it is shown to the user.

One model per cooling mode (forced / natural): they depend on different
variables and a single model would have to learn a discontinuity at
``v = 0``.

Run ``python -m pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.surrogate`` (``--help`` for the
sizes) to regenerate the dataset, retrain and write ``surrogate_<mode>.pt`` + its
trust report into ``--artifacts`` (default ``ARTIFACTS``: ``$PINNEAPPLE_HEATSINK_ARTIFACTS`` or
``~/.pinneapple/heatsink``). The HeatSink Sizer app keeps its trained copies in ``apps/heatsink_sizer/artifacts``
and passes that directory to :func:`load_surrogates`.

children.name: pinneapple_design.topology
pinneapple_design.topology.driver
children.doc:
Optimization loop: design variables -> (symmetry) -> density filter -> Heaviside projection -> problem.

    from pinneapple_design.topology import Compliance2D, DensityFilter, optimize
    prob = Compliance2D.mbb(60, 20)
    res = optimize(prob, volfrac=0.5, filt=DensityFilter.grid(60, 20, r_min=2.4), optimizer="oc")
    res.x_phys  # physical densities, res.history["objective"]

The volume constraint ``sum(v x_phys) <= volfrac sum(v)`` acts on the physical (projected) densities.
Extra constraints ``g(x_phys) <= 0`` (with gradients) can be given to MMA as callables. With
projection, ``beta`` is doubled every ``beta_every`` iterations up to ``beta_max`` (continuation).

Run density-based topology optimization of ``problem`` (see module docstring).

``optimizer``: ``"oc"`` (volume constraint only, non-increasing objectives such as compliance) or
``"mma"``. Stops when the largest design change is below ``tol`` (after the last ``beta`` step) or
after ``max_iter`` iterations.

``(value, gradient)``) at the entries ``idx``, central differences with step ``h``.

children.name: pinneapple_design.topology.filters
children.doc:
Density filter and Heaviside projection for density-based topology optimization.

Density filter (Bruns & Tortorelli 2001; Bourdin 2001): ``x_tilde = (H (v * x)) / (H v)`` with cone
weights ``H_ij = max(0, r_min - |c_i - c_j|)`` and element volumes ``v``. Works on any element
centroids (structured grids or the triangles of a rotor), built with a KD-tree.

Heaviside projection (Wang, Lazarov & Sigmund 2011)::

    x_bar = (tanh(beta eta) + tanh(beta (x_tilde - eta))) / (tanh(beta eta) + tanh(beta (1 - eta)))

``beta -> infinity`` gives a 0/1 design; ``beta`` is raised by continuation.

classes.sig: (centroids: np.ndarray, r_min: float, volumes: np.ndarray | None = None)
classes.doc: Linear density filter ``x_tilde = W x`` with ``W = diag(1/(H v)) H diag(v)``.

methods.doc: Filter on a structured ``nelx x nely`` grid, element ``e = i * nely + j``, size ``h``.

methods.name: backward
methods.doc: Chain rule: d/dx of a function of x_tilde with gradient ``g``.

classes.doc:
Element densities from fewer design variables: ``x_elem = S x_var`` (a 0/1 sparse matrix).

``rotational(centroids, n_fold)``: every element takes the variable of its image in the sector
``0 <= phi < 2 pi / n_fold`` (nearest centroid after rotation; exact on meshes with that symmetry).

children.name: pinneapple_design.topology.magnetic
children.doc:
Topology optimization of rotor iron for torque, on the 2D A_z machine model.

Design domain: the rotor-core elements of a
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machine.SPMMachine` (with ``magnet_thickness=0`` it is a
reluctance rotor; with magnets, the iron under them). Material interpolation on the reluctivity,
``nu = nu0 + rho^p (nu_iron(|B|^2) - nu0)`` (linear or nonlinear iron). The torque at each rotor angle is
the Maxwell-stress (Arkkio) torque of the model and its sensitivity comes from one adjoint solve per
angle with the Newton tangent (:meth:`SPMMachine.torque_and_design_gradient`).

Objectives (``evaluate`` returns a value to minimise):

* ``"mean"``: ``-mean_k T(theta_k) / T_ref`` -- maximise the average torque over the given angles;
* ``"ripple"``: ``std_k T(theta_k) / T_ref`` -- use with :meth:`RotorTorqueProblem.mean_torque_constraint`.

Currents follow the rotor synchronously: ``i_k = I cos(p theta + gamma - 2 pi k / 3)`` (``gamma`` is the
electrical angle of the current vector relative to the rotor's reference axis at ``theta = 0``).

classes.sig: (machine, thetas: Sequence[float], I_peak: float, gamma: float, objective: str = 'mean', T_ref: float = 1.0)

methods.name: torques
methods.doc: Torque at every angle and its gradient (n_angles, n) w.r.t. the physical densities.

methods.name: mean_torque_constraint
methods.doc: Constraint ``1 - mean(T) / T_min <= 0`` for :func:`~pinneapple_design.topology.optimize`.

children.name: pinneapple_design.topology.optimizers
children.doc:
Design-update rules: optimality criteria (OC) and the method of moving asymptotes (MMA).

OC: the classical fixed-point update for one volume constraint and a non-increasing objective
(compliance-type problems), with a bisection on the Lagrange multiplier.

MMA: K. Svanberg, "The method of moving asymptotes -- a new method for structural optimization",
Int. J. Numer. Meth. Eng. 24 (1987) 359-373. Each iteration replaces the objective and the
constraints ``f_i(x) <= 0`` by convex separable approximations ``r_i + sum p_ij/(U_j - x_j) + q_ij/(x_j - L_j)``
and solves the subproblem through its dual, a smooth concave maximization over ``lambda >= 0``
(here with L-BFGS-B). Elastic variables ``y_i >= 0`` with cost ``c y + y^2/2`` keep the subproblem
feasible (the dual then stays bounded). The coefficient and asymptote-update formulas follow the
paper and Svanberg's later public note on MMA/GCMMA (2007): ``p = (U-x)^2 (1.001 g+ + 0.001 g- + eps)``,
``q = (x-L)^2 (0.001 g+ + 1.001 g- + eps)``, asymptote factors 0.7 / 1.2 on oscillation / monotone steps.
This implementation is written from those formulas, not from any existing MMA code.

classes.name: MMA
classes.sig: (n: int, m: int, xmin = 0.0, xmax = 1.0, move: float = 0.5, asyinit: float = 0.5, asyincr: float = 1.2, asydecr: float = 0.7, c: float = 1000.0, d: float = 1.0)
classes.doc: Method of moving asymptotes for ``min f0(x)  s.t.  f_i(x) <= 0,  xmin <= x <= xmax``.

methods.name: update
methods.sig: (x: np.ndarray, f0: float, df0: np.ndarray, f: np.ndarray, df: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: New design from values and gradients at ``x``: ``f`` (m,), ``df`` (m, n).

functions.name: oc_update
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, dfdx: np.ndarray, dvdx: np.ndarray, volume_target: float, volume_of, move: float = 0.2, eta: float = 0.5, xmin: float = 0.0, xmax: float = 1.0)
functions.doc:
One OC step: ``x_new = clip(x (max(-df/dx, 0) / (lambda dv/dx))^eta)`` with ``volume_of(x_new) =
volume_target`` found by bisection on ``lambda``. ``volume_of`` maps design variables to the volume.

children.name: pinneapple_design.topology.problems
children.doc:
Density-based topology-optimization problems on structured grids of square bilinear (Q4) elements.

Grid convention: ``nelx x nely`` elements of size ``h``, element ``e = i * nely + j`` (i along x,
j along y, y upwards), node ``n = i * (nely + 1) + j``. Element matrices are integrated with 2x2
Gauss quadrature (selective one-point integration for the incompressibility penalty).

Every problem exposes ``n`` (number of elements), ``volumes`` and ``evaluate(x) -> (f, df/dx)`` on
physical densities ``x`` in [0, 1].

* :class:`Compliance2D` -- plane-stress linear elasticity, SIMP ``E = Emin + x^p (E0 - Emin)``,
  compliance ``c = f^T u``, ``dc/dx_e = -p x_e^(p-1) (E0 - Emin) u_e^T k_e u_e``. Presets:
  :meth:`Compliance2D.mbb` (half MBB beam) and :meth:`Compliance2D.cantilever`.
* :class:`ThermalCompliance2D` -- steady conduction ``k = kmin + x^p (1 - kmin)``, uniform heat source,
  isothermal sink on a boundary segment, objective ``f^T T``.
* :class:`StokesDissipation2D` -- Stokes flow in a Brinkman medium (Borrvall & Petersson, Int. J.
  Numer. Meth. Fluids 41 (2003) 77-107): inverse permeability
  ``alpha(x) = a_min + (a_max - a_min) q (1 - x) / (q + x)`` (x = 1 fluid), velocity-driven, objective the
  potential power ``0.5 u^T K u`` (viscous + Brinkman + incompressibility penalty) whose sensitivity is
  ``0.5 u_e^T (d alpha/dx_e) m_e u_e`` (the minimum of a quadratic energy over a fixed affine space).
  Incompressibility is imposed by a penalty with one-point (reduced) integration.

doc:
pinneapple_design — Geometry construction and physics-guided design optimization.

Sub-modules
-----------
geometry         (was pinneapple_geom)
    Geometry utilities: rich SDF library (20+ primitives), CSG operations,
    physics domains (2D & 3D channel, cavity, pipe, L-shape, annular, …),
    mesh generation (structured / SDF-based), mesh collocation for 3D PINNs,
    airfoil generation (NACA), RBF interpolation, and STL/STEP import.

design_optimizer  (was pinneapple_design_opt)
    Physics-guided design optimization: shape parametrization, adjoint solver,
    surrogate model, gradient / Bayesian / evolutionary optimizers, Pareto
    fronts (multi-objective), manufacturing constraints, and PINN refinement.

Integration helpers
-------------------
``build_domain(name, ...)``
    Wraps ``geometry.get_domain`` with fallback to get_domain_3d.
``sample_domain(domain, n_interior, n_boundary)``
    Returns interior and boundary collocation points from a domain object.
``optimize(param_space, surrogate, objective, ...)``
    One-shot design optimization shortcut backed by DesignOptLoop.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_design import build_domain, sample_domain, optimize
>>> domain = build_domain("lid_driven_cavity_2d")
>>> x_int, x_bnd = sample_domain(domain, 4096, 512)
>>> result = optimize(param_space, surrogate, drag_objective, method="bayesian")
